articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Nato condemns Moscow’s ‘irresponsible nuclear rhetoric’ as strikes on Kyiv intensify
articles.body:
- 
  Nato on Tuesday condemned “irresponsible nuclear rhetoric” by Russia, after Moscow warned it would “deploy its entire arsenal” if the alliance threatens its exclave Kaliningrad. “I can confirm that Russia sent a non-paper to Nato and that we have sent a response, noting that Nato is a defensive Alliance and none of our activities or exercises pose a risk to any part of Russia,” Allison Hart, a Nato spokesperson, said. “We strongly denounce the threat of force, including any irresponsible nuclear rhetoric. We call on Russia to end its unprovoked war in Ukraine.”
- 
  Russia has intensified daytime strikes on Kyiv using jet-powered drones that Ukrainian forces are struggling to intercept. Russia fired ballistic missiles and dozens of jet-powered drones at Kyiv, Ukraine’s air force said Tuesday, as Moscow seeks to make Ukraine buckle under the pressure of day-and-night bombardment of its capital and other cities. Russia has used new jet-powered drones that fly too fast and too high for Ukrainian ground-based air defenses to shoot down.
- 
  Russia struck two datacentres in Kyiv overnight, a military-linked cargo vessel in the Black Sea, and another vessel with military cargo in the Ukrainian port of Odesa, the Russian defence ministry said on Tuesday. In a later evening statement, the ministry said its forces had launched a drone strike on a ship in the Black Sea which it said was carrying cargo intended for the Ukrainian armed forces.
- 
  Ukraine’s top university on Tuesday said it was ordering students to stay home as it switched to remote classes due to the surge in Russian daytime drone attacks on the capital. Kyiv’s Taras Shevchenko National University said it would “switch to a remote format of work” until at least 16 October, “due to the deteriorating security situation in Kyiv”. The university’s main campus is close to the National Academy of Sciences, which was hit by a drone strike, killing one person, on Monday.
- 
  Russian glide bombs struck a school in the northern Ukrainian city of Sumy on Tuesday, killing two people and injuring six, the regional governor said. The city’s governor, Oleh Hryhorov, said three children were among the injured. He said teachers and school officials had managed to evacuate 100 people.
- 
  Russia’s foreign investment envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, met US officials in Washington for talks about future US-Russia energy projects planned after Moscow’s war against Ukraine, a US government official told AFP. Dmitriev and US officials held “constructive discussions on a peaceful resolution to the Russia-Ukraine conflict and possible US-Russia energy initiatives after the war ends” on Monday, the official said on Tuesday. “The visit follows special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner’s recent meeting with president Putin in Moscow and their discussions last week with Ukrainian officials in NYC,” said the official, speaking anonymously.
- 
  The US president, Donald Trump, favours a proposal under which the US would lift some sanctions if Russia released a number of political prisoners, according to a report in the Atlantic. The White House did not comment directly on the report. When asked about the article, a US official told AFP that Trump was “committed to continuing to play a constructive role in ending the war between Russia and Ukraine, and he remains optimistic that we’ll ultimately get a peace deal done”.
- 
  Russia will cut funding for welfare, education and healthcare in next year’s state budget to help cover soaring military spending, fiscal documents obtained by Reuters showed. Russia plans to spend 17.1tn roubles (US$202.58bn) on defence in 2027, about 27% more than the 13.5tn roubles originally budgeted and the highest figure since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022. Funding for social policy, which covers items such as state pensions, payments to war veterans and maternity benefits, will shrink by 7%, while education funding will fall by 6% and healthcare by 6.8%.
- 
  Belgium will transfer three F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine by the end of the year to help in its war with Russia, Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said on Tuesday. Zelenskyy said Ukraine had already received “urgent deliveries” of F-16 ammunition from Belgium and Spain, among other countries. Zelenskyy later said later Ukraine had received a “very good” assistance package the day before of a NASAMS air defence system, developed jointly in the US and Norway.
- 
  A Russian nuclear-capable strategic bomber crashed Tuesday on a training mission in the country’s far east, killing six members of its crew, its defence ministry said. The ministry said in a statement that the Tu-95 bomber went down in an unpopulated area in the Amur region, adding that one crew member survived the crash and was hospitalised with injuries.

articles.title: Live: Several people killed as Russia launches new round of strikes on Kyiv
articles.body:
Live: Ukraine’s grid operator orders emergency power cuts in Kyiv after Russian strikes
Ukraine's main energy provider DTEK said it had made emergency power cuts in Kyiv as directed by the national grid operator after Russia hit the country's infrastructure in a wave of deadly drone and missile strikes. At least seven people, including a 14-year-old child, were killed in the attacks, Ukrainian authorities said. Follow our liveblog for all the latest updates.
Vatican envoy visits Ukrainian prisoners of war in Russia
Papal envoy Cardinal Matteo Zuppi discussed humanitarian issues in the Ukraine war in talks with
Russian officials and visited Ukrainian prisoners of war, Russia's Foreign Ministry said.
Zuppi's three days of talks coincided with an appeal by Pope Leo XIV to Russia and Ukraine to sit down and discuss how to end the four-year war. The pontiff also decried national leaders who he said were "beginning to speak about nuclear weapons and wars that are becoming ever more destructive".
The Foreign Ministry said Zuppi met Kremlin foreign policy officer Yuri Ushakov and other Russian officials and discussed prospects for a settlement as well as humanitarian issues, including prisoner of war exchanges and displaced children.
The statement said Zuppi, head of the Italian bishops conference, also discussed conditions in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in Ukraine's Kherson region, where Ukrainian officials said Kyiv's military used drones last weekend to deliver food and medicine to civilians.
The Foreign Ministry statement said Ukraine was blocking all attempts to provide supplies to the town's residents. Ukrainian officials say Russian forces are preventing them from leaving the town.
Ukraine power operator announces emergency power cuts after Russian strikes
Ukraine's largest energy company said it had made some emergency power cuts in Kyiv after Russia hit the country's infrastructure in a wave of deadly drone and missile strikes.
"Emergency power outages have been implemented, following a directive from Ukrenergo," said DTEK, referring to the national grid operator.
No imminent threat to NATO territory from Russia, Rutte says
NATO's Secretary General Mark Rutte said there was no imminent threat to NATO territory from Russia, in response to a warning issued by Moscow over the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad.
The threat assessment regarding Russia was unchanged from three weeks, three months and a year ago, Rutte said, despite the warning sent to NATO by Moscow in a document seen by Reuters.
In the document, Russia said it would be ready to resort to nuclear weapons if the Western alliance attempted to cut off the territory, which is on the Baltic Sea sandwiched between Poland and Lithuania.
If Russia wanted to act against Finland, one of the Baltic nations, Poland or any other NATO country, it would be preceded by a military build-up, Rutte said at an event held by Euronews in Brussels.
He underlined the United States would stay involved in defending Europe by conventional and nuclear means.
Russia says European arms factories supplying Ukraine are legitimate military targets
Factories in Europe producing arms for Ukraine are legitimate military targets for Russia, Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said during a press briefing.
Zakharova said that European countries were directly involved in the conflict through their military support for Ukraine, adding that such activity delayed a resolution to the war.
She was responding to a question about Poland's apparent readiness to host a factory producing Patriot interceptor missiles for Ukraine.
Russian attacks bring Ukraine's steel production to a halt, union says
Ukraine, one of the world's 10 largest steel producers before Russia's full-scale invasion, has halted steel production after Russian attacks shut its remaining operating plants, the country's steel producers' union said.
"Steel is not currently being produced," the union told Reuters.
Ukraine produced 7.4 million metric tons of steel in 2025, down from 21.4 million tons in 2021. In 2021, metal exports generated nearly $14 billion and accounted for about 20 percent of the country's total exports.
Before 2014, Ukraine operated five major steel plants. One was seized after Russia occupied parts of the Donbas region in 2014, while two others were effectively destroyed during fighting for Mariupol in southern Ukraine following Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.
Until recently, steel production continued at ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih, the country's largest steelworks, at Metinvest-owned Zaporizhstal in the frontline city of Zaporizhzhia, and at several smaller plants.
But intensified Russian attacks in recent weeks have forced the plants to halt production.
ArcelorMittal said last week it had informed the Ukrainian government that "safe and sustainable" operations were no longer possible after four strikes in five weeks caused extensive damage and killed five workers at the southeastern plant.
Death toll from Russian bombing of Ukraine rises to seven, Zelensky says
Russia's attacks across Ukraine killed seven civilians and wounded two dozen more, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said, without providing details.
Sweden contributes fighter jets to NATO mission in Poland again
Sweden will from October deploy Gripen fighter jets to Poland as part of a NATO airspace surveillance mission, the Nordic country's government said.
The jets will contribute to the NATO military alliance's air and missile defence and protect a logistics hub in southeastern Poland that is used for military and civilian support to Ukraine, the Nordic country's government said
Sweden, which joined NATO in 2024, also in 2025 contributed jets to the mission
"The serious security situation and the recurring violations of NATO airspace show the need for high military readiness on the eastern flank," Defence Minister Pal Jonson said in a statement
The fighter jets, which are produced by Swedish defence group Saab, will mainly be based in Sweden while contributing to the mission, the government said
Zelensky says he visited military command post near Ukraine’s eastern frontline
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he visited a military command post near the eastern frontline on Wednesday.
Zelensky said he met servicemen who are fighting around the town of Lyman in the Donetsk region, where Ukraine has recently recaptured territory from Russian forces.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky, Commander-in-Chief of the Ukrainian Armed Forces Major General Mykhailo Drapatyi and Ukrainian Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara pose for a photo together with Ukrainian service members of the 66th Separate Mechanized Brigade near the front line in Donetsk region, Ukraine, September 30, 2026. Photo: Ukrainian Presidential Press Service via Reuters.
Putin will address newly-elected Duma later today
Russian President Vladimir Putin will deliver a speech in the newly-elected parliament later today, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.
Russia used 190 attack drones and ballistic missiles in overnight attacks, Zelensky says
“Since last night, emergency services and repair crews have been working to address the aftermath of the Russian strike. It was a difficult attack – nearly 190 attack drones, as well as ballistic missiles,” Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a post on X.
“And the main target was energy infrastructure in the capital and the Kyiv region.”
Ukraine death toll climbs to five, Zelensky says
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a post on X that at least five people were killed and 14 were injured in Russia’s latest attacks on Ukraine.
NATO denounces Moscow’s nuclear warning: ‘Irresponsible’
NATO spokesperson Allison Hart said the alliance has responded to Russia’s nuclear weapon warning.
“We strongly denounce the threat of force, including any irresponsible nuclear rhetoric. We call on Russia to end its unprovoked war in Ukraine,” she said.
A senior European defence official told Reuters that it was the first time since the Cold War “that Russia is threatening us like this. So this is serious.”
A NATO diplomat said: “I would say that the Russian letter is only another Russian attempt to intimidate Europeans, and that the response by NATO is firm and responsible. [It] reaffirms that we will not be dissuaded from supporting Ukraine.”
Russia issues nuclear warning to NATO as tensions rise in the Baltic
Russia has warned NATO it would be ready to resort to nuclear weapons if the Western alliance attempted to cut off Kaliningrad, a Russian exclave that borders the Baltic Sea.
In a document sent to NATO and seen by Reuters, Moscow accused the alliance of a “dangerous and reckless course” that entailed “high risks of the outbreak of a direct armed conflict”.
The document said this included the possibility “of Russian strikes against decision-making centres in the alliance’s member states right from the outset of the conflict”.
“Russia will be ready to use the entire arsenal of forces and capabilities at its disposal, including nuclear weapons, in order to defend its territory should NATO countries undertake any attempt aimed at isolating the Kaliningrad Region from the rest of the country,” said the text, classed as a “non-paper” – diplomatic jargon for an informal document.
Russia has launched mass attack campaign on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, PM says
Russia has moved to mass attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi, after the overnight strikes on energy facilities in the capital and other regions.
“This was the first time such a massive and combined attack had taken place since the end of the last heating season,” Koretskyi said on Telegram.
Death toll in Russian missile strikes in Ukraine climbs to four
Two women and a 14-year-old child died in overnight strikes on the Ukrainian capital and a town on the northern outskirts. Another person was killed in an attack on a Kyiv warehouse, the city’s Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
In pictures: Russia’s overnight attacks in Ukraine
A police officer and residents stand in front of a home that was heavily damaged during a Russian missile strike in the town of Vyshhorod, in the Kyiv region, on September 30, 2026.
Municipal employees prepare to transport the body of a resident killed in Russia’s missile strike on Vyshhorod.
A Vyshorod resident looks at the rubble that was once a garage.
All photos: Valentyn Ogirenko, Reuters
‘Dark winter’ for Europe amid Russia’s sabotage campaign, Belgian minister warns
Europe needs to rapidly improve its air defence as Russia continues its hybrid actions in the coming months, Belgium’s Defence minister Theo Francken warned at the Defence & Space Summit in Brussels.
“There will be more hybrid threat actions (in the) coming months. It will be a dark winter for Europe.” 
“We need to scale up our air defences and we need to have more stocks, scale up production. Everything has to go faster,” he said.
Ukraine’s war costs for 2026 expected to hit €135 billion
Ukraine’s total war costs will reach an estimated €135 billion this year, the country’s Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said.
Koretskyi said the government is working to close a €24 billion funding gap to ensure it can conduct active combat operations at the start of 2027. Some of it will be covered by austerity measures, he said; but for the bulk part, help from partners will be needed.
This is the first time Kyiv has released an estimate of its annual war costs. There are no comparable figures for 2025.
Russia extends diesel export ban until end of October
The Russian government has extended a ban on diesel exports for fuel producers until the end of October.
Russia introduced restrictions on exports of gasoline, jet fuel and diesel because of domestic fuel shortages exacerbated by Ukrainian drone strikes on oil refineries.
(FRANCE 24 with AP, AFP and Reuters)

articles.title: Western F-16s promised safe skies over Kiev: Why could they all go MIA soon?
articles.body:
Western F-16s promised safe skies over Kiev: Why could they all go MIA soon?
Ukraine’s NATO-donated F-16 fleet is out of commission more often than it engages Russian drones, The Wall Street Journal has claimed.
The American-produced fighter jets were touted as the latest “gamechanger” weapon in Kiev’s conflict with Russia, a tool that will help “achieve goals outside of Ukraine,” as Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said when the first batch was set to arrive in the summer of 2024.
However, a key EU member in the European-led scheme cannot keep up with necessary maintenance of the fleet, according to the newspaper.
What is the F-16 initiative?
The plan was launched in 2023, as Ukraine’s fleet of Soviet-built military aircraft was dwindling. Pro-Kiev propaganda implied that the US-made multirole jets would help Ukrainian forces challenge Russia’s air dominance over the front line. But it was hardly a secret that they would be kept far away from Russian SAMs and fighter jets and only engage long-range drones and cruise missiles.
Donor nations announced they were prepared to spend years training Ukrainian pilots, refurbishing the aircraft they were willing to spare, and happily signing deals for modern replacements to bolster their own militaries – the F-16 initiative was effectively a NATO-backed pyramid scheme allowing everyone to spend big and upgrade their air forces.
Ukraine has since received about 40 jets, roughly half of what the donors pledged, and lost several of them during combat missions, reportedly after corners were cut for expediency during training courses. It is now facing winter with an acute shortage of air defense systems.
What’s the problem?
Belgium’s Sabena Aerospace Engineering, awarded a $235.5 million contract for maintenance of Ukraine’s F-16 fleet, is not keeping up with the demand, according to the Wall Street Journal editorial board.
An inspection that normally takes two to six weeks lasts “as long as 40 weeks in Belgium,” retired US Navy Rear Admiral Mark Montgomery said. Another Western source said more than half of Ukrainian jets are now in maintenance limbo, with the rest set to become grounded by the end of the year.
Was the issue unexpected?
Media reports saying that the Ukrainian F-16 fleet is being overworked surfaced as early as July, as Kiev’s shortage of ground-launched interceptor missiles became more acute. There were also indicators pointing to a bottleneck in Belgium.
In April, the Norwegian Broadcasting Corporation reported that not one of the six F-16s that Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store pledged to Ukraine in 2023 had been delivered. Four of them were not airworthy to begin with, but the two others were previously used to train Ukrainian pilots in Denmark.
The six jets were stuck at a Sabena workshop in Belgium due to “significant capacity problems,” the report said.
Is Ukraine getting more jets?
There were delays in deliveries as well.
Belgium promised in 2024 to transfer 30 aircraft set to be phased out by its air force, which was expecting F-35 replacements. Then-Defense Minister Ludivine Dedonder said Ukraine would start receiving the old jets “as soon as the F-35s arrive on Belgian soil,” but no transfers have been reported since.
Most of the aircraft that Kiev did get reportedly came from the Netherlands and Denmark, the co-leaders of the F-16 initiative.
Why does Ukraine have air defense problems?
A shortage of Western weapons partially caused Ukraine’s current situation.
When this summer Vladimir Zelensky announced a 40-day “pressure campaign” of long-rage strikes on refineries, civilian ships, and commercial warehouses, his team reportedly hoped that images of smoke-plumes stretching over big Russian cities would support his bid to receive more Patriot missile interceptors from the limited US stockpile.
If true, the plan backfired. NATO nations are scrambling to provide what Kiev wants, while the economic damage caused by Russian retaliation is mounting. And Ukraine already has a $27 billion military budget hole that European donors are struggling to fill.
Ukrainian forces previously learned that Western arms gifts come with caveats. Donated NATO artillery systems lacked interoperability and were described as a “zoo” by troops. Much-hyped NATO battle tanks turned out to be mostly useless in drone-driven warfare and had to be kept away from the front line.
Can Ukraine come up with alternatives?
Zelensky puts on a brave face talking about the dire situation. Last week he claimed Ukraine had successfully tested four new interceptor drones designed to shoot down faster-moving jet UAVs – the kind of targets the WSJ claimed F-16s are well-suited to take down.
But an earlier Reuters report said trials in July “did not go to plan” as the prototypes lost control and “crashed into nearby fields and forests.”
Ukrainian opposition lawmaker Sergey Rakhmanin, who sits on the national defense committee, has said Kiev missed Russia’s rapid development of jet kamikaze drones. He said Ukrainian interceptors cost up to $100,000 apiece and that scaling up production would require too much time, even if funding becomes available.

articles.title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1679: Russia raises its war budget by 27% to a record as it looks to grow its war in 2027
articles.body:
Exclusives
Military
Russia drained the Kakhovka Reservoir. Now it hides in the dry bed to creep toward Zaporizhzhia. A frontline commander expects small Russian groups to slip into the city by winter. A leading analyst calls that far too categorical—and says the front is moving the other way.
Vivaldi counteroffensive advanced after Ukraine took Russia’s drones out of the fight, ISW assesses. Armored vehicles reached heavy Russian fortifications in the Lyman sector without coming under drone attack, which the analysts read as a sign of Ukrainian drone overmatch.
Russia’s mass drone attacks on Ukraine have a goal—likely Ukraine’s capitulation by spring 2027, ISW says. Until his new theory of victory has played out, Putin is unlikely to soften his demands or enter serious ceasefire talks, according to ISW.
Russia’s pipeline into Kupiansk is now its escape route—with kidnapped civilians as human shields, Ukraine says. Ukrainian drones filmed the column on 27 September. Khartia warned Russia could pass the footage off as an "evacuation" or "rescue" of civilians.
Ukraine makes local gains on Pokrovsk front despite sustained Russian attacks. The marines cleared 5 square kilometers and captured two Russian soldiers.
A Ukrainian Hornet drone hit a Russian radar 120 km behind the front. It was likely a $100 million Nebo-M. The strike is part of a push to cut Russian logistics and strip Russian forces of radar and electronic warfare systems, a brigade officer says.
Ukraine hits railways of Bryansk, Russia’s launchpad for strikes on Kyiv: downed bridge and 28 derailed cars, region’s governor says. Ukraine's drones reportedly hit the region's railways.
Intelligence and technology
Mavic vs Slavic: Ukrainian developers adapt reconnaissance drones to the modern battlefield. “The drone was developed as a Ukrainian alternative to Chinese commercial quadcopters,” Vyriy Industries said.
A Ukrainian firm now rents out drone jammers by the day—but the deposit is the device’s full price. The daily fee comes off a deposit worth the whole device—rent long enough and the jammer becomes yours.
Ukraine just caught a Geran-5 at 425 km/h—the jet drone that has often outrun Ukrainian interceptor drones since January. Ukrainian crews now stop just over half of Russia's jet-powered drones, against more than 90% of the older Shaheds, even as Moscow builds them by the thousand.
Russia is stepping up fake Ukrainian government pages as bait for recruiting agents, Ukraine’s security service says. Russian intelligence uses the counterfeits to spread disinformation and to harvest data on the Ukrainians who subscribe.
Russia is launching a faster Geran-5 at Ukraine that satellite jamming may no longer knock off course, a monitoring channel says. The drone can steer by images of the terrain below, and its extra speed makes it harder for interceptors to catch, though Ukrainian officials have not confirmed the system.
International
Russia ordered arson attack on Estonian military robot-maker supplying Ukraine, Estonia confirms. Estonia says its intelligence service established that Russia’s special services ordered the August fire at Milrem Robotics, as Russian sabotage operations spreads across Europe.
Belgium rushes three F-16s to Ukraine as Russia expands its drone and missile assault. Zelenskyy says the aircraft will arrive by the end of 2026, strengthening Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian air targets and conduct combat missions.
Russian jet-powered drone hits near Yahodyn, just 1.5 km from Poland, as Warsaw changes air defense rules. Poland plans to allow decisions to engage aerial targets based on radar data.
Lithuania gets its US tank battalion back while the Pentagon weighs pulling up to 40,000 troops from Europe. The Lithuanian leader calls the decision an encouragement and says fewer American soldiers will remain on the continent overall.
Humanitarian and social impact
Russian troops enter homes and threaten starving Oleshky residents for food and alcohol, officials say. Residents who escaped the occupied Kherson Oblast city describe threats and abuse by Russian troops amid severe shortages of food, water, and medicine.
Russian mercenaries blew off African prisoners’ legs to practice battlefield medicine, Wagner fighter says. A Russian mercenary captured by Ukraine describes alleged Wagner training sessions where prisoners were deliberately maimed and killed so recruits could practice battlefield medicine and killing techniques.
Russia hits a Kharkiv high-rise overnight, injuring 43 people, then kills four in daylight strikes on central Kyiv and Dnipro. A pre-dawn strike on Ukraine's second city gave way to drone attacks on a business center and then a national science institution during working hours.
Political and legal developments
Russia raises its war budget by 27% and expands the army again – both to new records – even as its budget deficit widens and oil revenues fall. Moscow plans to spend a record 17.1 trillion rubles on defense in 2027 as it raises taxes and borrowing to cover a widening deficit.
The Kremlin calls mobilization talk “nonsense”—Zelenskyy says it has already begun, with North Korean reinforcements. The claim comes from Ukraine's military intelligence, which has tracked Russian preparations for a larger call-up for months.
War is costing Ukraine $155 billion per year. With Western aid running late, Kyiv is freezing everything but army, pensions, and public wages. Kyiv froze parks, fountains, and road repairs to pay its army and pensioners first.
After Russia hits Kyiv’s Academy of Sciences with jet-powered drone, the Kremlin says Ukraine must “pay a price”. Peskov calls Russia's intensified strikes part of that price.

articles.title: Japan wants to stand up to Russia. Can it stand on its own?
articles.body:
Japan wants to stand up to Russia. Can it stand on its own?
A 15-meter-high bronze memorial towers over the Amur River embankment: a Soviet soldier swings his rifle butt, smashing a Japanese border marker bearing the Imperial Chrysanthemum emblem – a symbol held sacred in Japan.
On September 4 – the day following Victory Day over Militaristic Japan and the End of WWII (as observed in Russia) – the Victory in the East memorial was unveiled at the highest point of the Amur River embankment in Khabarovsk. The monument was created at the initiative of Russian President Vladimir Putin, with the participation of the Russian Military Historical Society and the government of Khabarovsk Krai. The stone border post is an exact replica of a border stone erected by Japan on Sakhalin after the Russo-Japanese War.
The following day, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi demanded the removal of the monument. The depiction of the smashed chrysanthemum, she wrote on X, was absolutely unacceptable and was an affront to the national sentiments of the Japanese people. Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi called the monument “unacceptable” and deeply regrettable, and said that Tokyo would continue to press for its removal.
Moscow responded that it would not dismantle or alter the monument. Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova even stated that one might as well demand that the wind stop blowing or the sun stop shining.
Beijing seized the opportunity to remind its neighbor of past crimes: Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning advised Japan to learn from history, make a definitive break with militarism, and earn the trust of its neighbors through concrete actions.
At first glance, the situation appears unprecedented. In the span of a single month, the Russian president made a historic visit to Iturup; both sides summoned ambassadors; Japan, the US, and Australia held military exercises just 20 kilometers from the Russian border; and now, there’s the issue with the monument and the demand to tear it down. Media outlets speak of a “sharp chill” in relations, a new wave of confrontation in the Russian Far East, and even a potential “second front” of the Cold War.
However, Russian experts who spoke to RT view the situation differently.
A series of coincidences
The situation was triggered not by Russia’s actions, but by the Japanese Ministry of Defense.
On August 4, the Cabinet of Japan approved its annual Defense of Japan White Paper – a record-breaking 598 pages featuring an anime-style cover showing a group of smiling young people against the backdrop of a futuristic city. This year’s theme was “Security for the Future.” The content of the whitepaper was quite pragmatic, however. China was identified as Japan’s greatest strategic challenge; on this list, China was followed by Russia and North Korea; for the first time, the buildup of military power was directly linked to economic prosperity (hence the peaceful cover design).
There is a section on Russian military activity in the Far East: the document notes Tu-95 flights, 214 interceptions of Russian aircraft over the course of the year, the expansion of joint naval patrols with China (in August 2025, a submarine participated in these patrols for the first time), as well as a flight by Russian and Chinese bombers to the area near Shikoku Island in December. There is also a chapter on new methods of warfare, such as the use of mass-produced, low-cost drones and AI in decision-making. For the second consecutive year, the document characterizes Russian military actions in the Southern Kuril Islands as “illegal occupation.”
Nine days later, on August 13, Vladimir Putin visited Iturup. Throughout his years in office, the Russian president had never visited the southern islands of the Kuril chain, which are also claimed by Japan.
Japan’s reaction was immediate. Takaichi called the visit “absolutely unacceptable,” Motegi repeated Tokyo’s position about the islands being an “inherent part of Japanese territory,” and the Japanese Foreign Ministry summoned Russian Ambassador to Japan Nikolay Nozdrev. Moscow responded firmly, dismissing the statements of Japanese officials as politically irrelevant, offensive, and legally null and void; it reiterated that Iturup, like the rest of the Kurils, is an integral part of Russia, and that Japanese officials have no right to tell Moscow which regions of the country the Russian president may visit.
On August 15, the anniversary of Japan’s surrender in WWII, Takaichi sent a ‘tamagushi’ (ritual offering) to the Yasukuni Shrine. However, she refrained from going there personally, and the ruling party clarified that the donation was made from personal funds and in Takaichi’s capacity as LDP leader, rather than as head of government. The gesture was calculated to satisfy the domestic audience, without triggering a diplomatic row with Beijing and Seoul.
On August 18, Japanese Ambassador to Russia Akira Muto was summoned to the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin lodged a strong protest regarding statements made by the Japanese prime minister and foreign minister, asserting that Russia’s sovereignty and jurisdiction over the Southern Kuril Islands are inviolable, and that any attempts to call this reality into question are unacceptable and illegitimate.
On August 31, another incident occurred, this time involving military exercises. From September 8-24, Japan, the US, and Australia conducted Exercises Orient Shield with some operations taking place on Hokkaido Island, near the Russian border. The Japanese side was informed that provocative military activity near Russia’s Far Eastern borders is absolutely unacceptable; Zakharova specifically noted plans to deploy US land-based Typhon missile systems – capable of firing medium-and shorter-range missiles – during the exercises and warned of compensatory countermeasures.
On September 4, the monument was unveiled in Khabarovsk. That same day, the UN General Assembly voted to adopt the Equal Earth Projection. Japan voted in favor. But a few days later, it demanded a correction: on the online version of the new map, the four Southern Kuril Islands were shaded the same color as the rest of Russia, which Japan found unacceptable.
So there we have it – six incidents in 30 days. Each incident compounds the previous one, and together they form a picture of rapidly deteriorating relations.
Below, Russian experts analyze the situation.
‘Relations have not cooled suddenly’
Vasily Shchepkin – a Japanologist with a PhD in History, senior researcher of the Far East Department at the Institute of Oriental Manuscripts of the Russian Academy of Sciences, and an associate professor at the Higher School of Economics in St. Petersburg – suggests reframing the question.
“In my view, relations between Russia and Japan have not cooled suddenly; they have been in this state for over four years, since the start of Russia’s military operation in Ukraine. Japan joined Western sanctions, and everything that has happened over the past four years is largely a consequence of that,” he said.
Therefore, the rift happened not in September 2026, but in March 2022 – when Tokyo backed the collective West’s sanctions regime, and Moscow responded by withdrawing from peace treaty negotiations, cancelling visa-free travel for Japanese citizens to the Kuril Islands, and halting dialogue on joint economic activity there. Everything that followed was the consequence of that single decision.
So, what happened in August? According to Shchepkin, the current chain of events was a direct result of Putin’s visit to Iturup. Tokyo’s reaction was inevitable. However, he draws attention to a neglected detail. “Aside from statements, no concrete measures have followed so far.”
No actions were undertaken by Japan in September. No new sanctions packages were adopted; diplomats were not expelled, and the remaining projects were not cancelled. As for démarches, the summoning of diplomats, and declarations of unacceptable behavior, all this is standard diplomatic procedure.
“Neither Tokyo nor Moscow seeks to aggravate relations further,” Shchepkin says. “In my view, [relations] are unlikely to deteriorate further, because, speaking of bilateral interaction, neither side wants to halt it or escalate tensions.”
Therefore, we may conclude that Russia-Japan relations, in their current form, are a dependent variable.
“The current state of relations is rather a consequence of other events, which are not directly tied to the Russian-Japanese agenda,” the expert says.
An independent bilateral agenda no longer exists; therefore, we may only speak of the global situation and how it relates to Russia’s Far East.
“We are currently in a sort of deadlock which we return to whenever the global situation gets worse – and particularly when relations between Russia and the US deteriorate,” the expert says. “The US has long been the ‘third force’ on which Russia-Japan relations largely depended.”
Who started it?
While it’s true that relations are frozen, there is no consensus among the parties on who is to blame for this. Russian experts, however, have a clear opinion.
Olga Bonch-Osmolovskaya, a Japanologist with a PhD in History, describes the reasons behind Tokyo’s decision. According to her, after 2022, Japan’s policy ceased to be truly independent. But that is only part of the story.
“It is one thing to politically condemn a distant war and state one’s position for the sake of appearances, given the existence of a sort of ‘suzerain’; it is quite another to actively integrate oneself into the corresponding policy,” she says. Japan chose the latter option. And it did so with particular zeal.
“Driven by what one might call the ‘straight-A student complex’ of the Japanese and their tendency to be highly conscientious, sometimes even fanatical in executing tasks, Japan closely aligned itself with this course, joining the full package of sanctions against Moscow and withdrawing from various forms of cooperation,” Bonch-Osmolovskaya says.
The former policy – one that allowed Tokyo to balance between allied obligations and its own interests in the north – was curtailed. Along with it, all the achievements of the previous decade came to naught.
“Russia did not initiate the deterioration of relations with Japan,” Bonch-Osmolovskaya says. “It responded and continues to respond to Japanese sanctions and to the increased US military presence.”
There is a fine line between words and capabilities, however. Take Exercises Orient Shield, for example. “During the exercises, all sorts of maneuvers are practiced – the landing of troops, the transfer of ammunition, the deployment of HIMARS systems, air defense systems, etc.”
This explains Russia’s strong reaction. “Of course, no one is saying that this is literally preparation for an attack on the Kuril Islands. But Russia is obliged to evaluate not only statements, but military capabilities,” Bonch-Osmolovskaya says.
Intentions change along with governments, but military infrastructure remains. And military officials all over the world take this into account.
The result is a vicious circle: Japan builds up its military potential jointly with the US; in response, Russia strengthens its position in the Far East; then, Tokyo presents this strengthening as an additional justification for further militarization. And the circle repeats itself.
This is confirmed by Japan’s military spending. Japan crossed the 2% defense spending threshold ahead of schedule, a year earlier than the mark outlined in the 2022 strategy. For the current fiscal year, defense spending amounted to a record 8.8 trillion yen, and the request for the next year is already a record 8.9 trillion yen (about $56 billion). In June, the parliament renamed the Air Self-Defense Force into the Air and Space Self-Defense Force; this was the first renaming of one of the three branches of the Self-Defense Forces since their creation in 1954. In August, Takaichi announced further changes: the creation of a Space Operations Group, a Space Domain Awareness (SDA) satellite, and the expansion of the Okinawa Ground Self-Defense Force’s 15th Brigade into a division.
These actions are mainly directed against Beijing. But considering the geography, they are also directed against Moscow.
Energy instead of diplomacy
Despite all this, there is something that balances the dramatic picture. While diplomats are exchanging demarches, gas carriers are departing from Sakhalin and transporting LNG to Japan.
The Sakhalin-2 project survived sanctions, frozen political dialogue, and demands to dismantle the monument. In June, the US Office of Foreign Assets Control once again extended the special license until December 18, 2026. Such an exception has been issued annually since 2022, and each time it was preceded by negotiations between Tokyo and Washington. Russian LNG, according to the Japanese Ministry of Economy, provided about 9% of Japanese liquefied gas imports in 2025; According to Bonch-Osmolovskaya, the inverse relationship is even stronger – Japan accounted for about 58% of the project’s exports.
Vladimir Nelidov – PhD in History, associate professor of the Department of Oriental Studies at MGIMO, Senior Researcher at the Center for Japanese Studies at the Institute of Oriental Studies of the Russian Academy of Sciences, and RIAC expert – considers this to be the main reason why the threats didn’t go beyond words.
“Severing diplomatic relations would be disproportionate,” he says. “The possibilities for introducing additional economic sanctions are also limited: Japan does not have much leverage. For example, it remains involved in Sakhalin oil and gas projects and, I believe, is not ready to sacrifice them.”
Notably, the US administration insisted on Japan’s withdrawal from the Sakhalin projects. However, Tokyo remained. “As far as we can judge, Takaichi either convinced the US or insisted [on doing things her way] and so, despite the position of its senior ally, Japan remained in the projects.”
The second possible lever is humanitarian. Tokyo tries to preserve it, too. “The Japanese side has invested a lot of effort in humanitarian cooperation with Russia. Before the current escalation, the Japanese even proudly said that, despite the lack of political dialogue, cultural festivals and other events continue between the countries.” And Nelidov adds, “in the long term, Japan has perhaps more need for such contacts than Russia.”
Shchepkin supports this idea, adding that even in the past four years, and thanks to the efforts of the pro-Russia lobby within the Japanese Foreign Ministry, cooperation has been preserved in areas like culture, education, and tourism. The current flow of Russian tourists to Japan, the expert adds, is largely a legacy of the Shinzo Abe administration, when the parties agreed to put the territorial issue aside and focus on the economy, culture, and visas.
The general picture is quite clear. Bonch-Osmolovskaya calls it “cold peace” and warns that a complete rupture of relations would not benefit either country: while Japan could technically replace Sakhalin gas, doing so would require time, money, and even greater dependence on US suppliers, whereas Russia would lose revenue from the project. “A definitive break, should it occur, would come at too high a price for both sides,” she says.
Therefore, the limit to how far relations can deteriorate is not determined by diplomacy. It is dictated by the energy balance, and this applies to both parties.
Why Takaichi could not remain silent
A pressing question remains: why did the Japanese Prime Minister issue all these loud statements if no concrete measures were to follow?
Nelidov suggests viewing the situation through the eyes of the Japanese leadership to better understand their logic. Sanae Takaichi rose to power as a nationalist politician and, among other things, a defender of national honor. Her policy is grounded in this.
“Had she failed to react to the Russian president’s visit to the territory claimed by Japan, to the installation of the monument – which [Russia] views as fine, necessary, and valuable, but which the Japanese see as a desecration of a state symbol – or to the military exercises, she would have been torn apart, figuratively speaking, by her own party,” the expert says.
For example, when the US administration imposed sanctions against the International Criminal Court – including its presiding judge, Japanese national Tomoko Akane – Takaichi faced criticism for not standing up for her compatriot firmly enough. “If public opinion and fellow party members demand decisive action from her even in dealings with the US, then what would they say about Russia?”
A scenario in which Tokyo would have remained silent to avoid damaging relations with Moscow is virtually impossible.
Valery Kistanov, head of the Center for Japanese Studies at the Institute of China and Contemporary Asia of the Russian Academy of Sciences, drew attention to the details of the protest against the monument in Khabarovsk. Takaichi posted her comment on social media but did not issue an official statement, and major Japanese media outlets (except for right-wing conservative publications) barely covered the story. It didn’t cause a nationwide outcry.
In other words, the statement was addressed not to Moscow, but to fellow party members and the segment of the Japanese electorate for whom the events of 1945 remain an enduring historical wound. The offering made at Yasukuni on August 15 followed the same logic: made from personal funds and without Takaichi herself present, it was intended as a signal to the domestic audience, but was carefully calibrated to avoid provoking a new crisis in relations with Beijing.
The fact that the series of incidents was not followed by any practical actions holds the key to understanding the events of September. This means that a large part of what happened did not concern bilateral relations but was intended for domestic audiences.
However, this does not render the situation entirely harmless. Symbolic commitments tend to become entrenched: a prime minister who has demanded the dismantling of a monument cannot refute their own statement, and a successor would have to start from the same position.
Who benefits?
Experts agree on who benefits from the conflict, though they differ on the implications. “It is clear that the US is the primary beneficiary,” says Bonch-Osmolovskaya. “The worse relations between Moscow and Tokyo become, the stronger Japan’s existing dependence on the US grows in all aspects: weaponry, intelligence, supplies, and security guarantees.” Washington gains a disciplined ally, additional bases for the deployment of forces, and another tool for exerting pressure on the Russian Far East.
However, she adds, “It is important not to reduce the situation to a scenario where the US is some sort of ‘dark empire’ and Japan is merely its puppet.”
In Japan, there are certain beneficiaries of this confrontation as well. Among the proponents of revising post-war restrictions is the defense establishment, which Bonch-Osmolovskaya characterizes as revanchist and nationalistic, and arms manufacturers, for whom expanded exports open up markets that had been closed for nearly 80 years. The image of an external threat serves as a mechanism for legitimization: the longer the list of threats, the easier it is for the parliament to increase military spending and lift export restrictions.
Bonch-Osmolovskaya gives a rather harsh assessment and makes a historical analogy. She believes that the current propaganda is reminiscent of the decades preceding WWII, when Japan designated China as its primary adversary and demonized it; today, a similar process is unfolding regarding Russia. At the root of this, she sees the unresolved trauma of 1945: while the cult of the emperor was formally dismantled and the atrocities of the military machine were acknowledged, the defeat was never truly accepted, and strategic sovereignty was lost.
Nelidov takes a more measured approach, offering a different view that does not suggest malicious intent. The problem, he believes, is the so-called ‘security dilemma’ – a long-standing concept in international relations theory. A state strengthens its defenses; its neighbors, unaware of its true intentions, interpret this as preparation for aggression and arm themselves in response; the first state observes these preparations and continues its military buildup. “The paradox of the security dilemma is that in seeking to protect itself, the state ultimately finds itself in an even more dangerous situation,” he explains.
Another factor also comes into play. “Most Japanese diplomats, politicians, and even military officials have no desire to develop an independent view of the global situation,” Nelidov says, describing Japanese political circles as highly compliant pupils of the West; the few who acknowledge that the situation in Ukraine might be more complex than the prevailing narrative risk becoming outcasts. These sentiments did not emerge in 2022; they were shaped throughout the post-war period by the media and the education system, initially as anti-Soviet views. In Japanese opinion polls, Russia consistently ranks low in terms of public favorability, alongside China and North Korea.
Freezing point
If the current situation resembles ‘freezing point’, it is logical to ask what might drive the relations between Japan and Russia below freezing.
Bonch-Osmolovskaya mentions a specific threshold. “The next stage of deterioration could be the deployment of US long-range systems in Japan,” she says. Russia’s reaction would be predictable: a further military buildup on the Kuril Islands and in Sakhalin. A further contraction of economic ties is also likely; she believes that the fishing industry would suffer first, followed by what remains of trade.
Bonch-Osmolovskaya does not predict a direct military conflict. According to her, if it were to occur at all, it would happen only as part of a larger clash between Russia and the US or a major crisis surrounding Taiwan that dragged in all the neighboring states. In other words, a Russo-Japanese war is impossible as a standalone event – it could only be an episode within someone else’s war.
Nelidov views the situation somewhat differently. He points out that Japan’s defense policy identifies China and North Korea as the primary threats, with Russia ranking third on the list. But even when it comes to China and North Korea, it’s not about direct confrontation but rather an arms race. While this is certainly a negative phenomenon, it is fundamentally different from a direct conflict.
The comparison the expert draws with Europe is interesting. He considers the rhetoric of Berlin, London, Helsinki, and Stockholm far more threatening than that of Tokyo, which demonstrates “virtually no real readiness for aggressive action against Russia.” He is convinced there are certain limits the Japanese side will not cross.
He attributes East Asia’s greater reluctance to engage in direct conflict to accumulated experience: territorial disputes and mutual historical grievances are common in the region, and the elites have learned to manage such crises. For example, following Takaichi’s November statement regarding potential intervention in Taiwan, Tokyo’s relations with Beijing plummeted to their lowest point in a decade, and China imposed economic restrictions; yet within a few months, the situation had stabilized.
“In East Asia, I don’t see the kind of crazy Russophobia and readiness to direct all resources into the conflict that we’re witnessing in Europe,” says Nelidov. “Japan doesn’t intend to go to war with Russia; and neither does Russia want war with Japan. Both sides realize it is not in their interests. There are no strategically vital or fundamental contradictions between them.”
Is there a way to achieve a thaw in relations? All three experts agree that there is no simple solution. Normalizing bilateral ties is impossible until relations between Russia and the West are normalized; the Japanese leadership lacks both the will and the capacity to adopt an independent stance. However, Shchepkin believes that once the conflict in Ukraine ends, Tokyo will be among the first to act: as soon as the sanctions regime is lifted or minimized, Japan will be ready to soften its position and resume dialogue.
However, the opinions of experts diverge when it comes to assessing the current pause in relations. For Nelidov, it is merely another fluctuation in a long history of regional squabbles. For Bonch-Osmolovskaya, it represents a deeper rift: Russia is asserting itself as an independent civilization, while Japan, in response, is becoming increasingly integrated into the US system of control over Eurasia. She advocates neither for reconciliation at any cost nor for territorial concessions, but rather for maintaining energy, economic, and cultural ties as a bridge – “not so much with the Japan of today, but with the Japan that might one day become more independent.”
As Bonch-Osmolovskaya concludes, “Japan cannot simultaneously be an independent civilization and America’s forward military outpost. It will have to make a choice.”

articles.title: From nuclear to hybrid: The key moments from the Euronews Defence Summit
articles.body:
Euronews hosted on Wednesday its first Defence and Space Summit. Here are the key moments from the day-long gathering, bringing together the NATO Secretary General, ministers, senior officials and industry leaders.
Is Europe ready to defend itself?
That was the central question at the Euronews Defence and Space Summit, which brought together policymakers, lawmakers and industry leaders as Europe grapples with the need to rearm and deter potential threats.
Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine has transformed Europe's security landscape, exposing longstanding weaknesses and forcing governments to rethink defence spending, military capabilities and industrial capacity.
As Russia continues its war in Ukraine and hybrid attacks against European allies increase, the pressure to act is growing.
Here are five key moments from Wednesday's summit.
Radev raises the alarm
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev was among the day's most anticipated speakers. On Wednesday, he challenged the EU's strategy of supporting Ukraine, describing it as a failed attempt at "peace by force".
"The war in Ukraine challenged our critical thinking and realistic approach," he said.
"It challenged our ability to assess the strategic centre of gravity of the opponent. It challenged most of all our ability to design feasible political objectives and to translate them into a sound military strategy and to define a desired end state."
Radev called for greater diplomatic engagement with the Kremlin to end the war and avert what he described as the "worst-case scenario" of a nuclear attack against Europe.
Russia controls the world's largest nuclear arsenal, with an estimated 4,400 stockpiled warheads, including 1,796 strategically deployed.
"There is a nuclear card," Radev said.
"We need to have this into account. We cannot close our eyes (to the fact) that there are nuclear weapons on our continent, there are nuclear weapons in the arsenal of Russia. And this is part of the game calculation."
His remarks came hours after Reuters reported that Russia had sent a document threatening to "use the entire arsenal of forces and capabilities at its disposal, including nuclear weapons" to defend its territory.
Rutte reassures allies
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte followed Radev with a very different message for Moscow: "Stop the nuclear threats."
Rutte declined to comment on the reported document but offered a glimpse of NATO's response to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"Putin knows he can never win (against) NATO, so I don't take this seriously," he said. "Of course, we had to reply and make clear to him that NATO is a defensive alliance."
"I think the best way to deal with this is to have a bit of calm," he added.
Rutte also addressed the rise in hybrid attacks targeting Ukraine's allies, including an arson attack at a robotics defence company in Estonia and an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport in Germany.
He described the incidents as attempts by Putin to divert attention from the stalled battlefield, fracture Western unity and weaken military support for Kyiv.
Seeking to reassure allies, Rutte said: "There is no immediate threat to NATO territory."
"We will defend every inch of NATO territory, every square kilometre, square mile," he said. "There's no doubt Putin knows this. So that threat is not there. And if anything happens, we are ready to counter it."
Rutte praised Ukraine's gains on the battlefield and its deep strikes inside Russia, but highlighted a critical weakness: air defence.
Russia has used sustained aerial attacks to pummel Ukrainian cities, putting pressure on Kyiv's stocks of air defence interceptors.
"It is crucial now to keep Ukraine strong," Rutte said, urging allies to provide Patriot interceptors. "But Ukraine is not doing worse (now) than some time ago."
Francken warns of 'dark winter'
Despite the reassurances, concern over Europe's security is growing.
Belgian Defence Minister Theo Francken warned that Europe was facing a "dark winter" of increasing interference.
"Russia, air attack, air attack, air attack. This is the biggest threat. So we need air defence, air defence, air defence," Francken told the summit.
"We need to have more stocks, more production, scale up production, and a large industrial base. Everything has to go faster."
Francken said Russia had decades of experience in hybrid warfare and argued that Europe should draw on Ukraine's battlefield expertise to keep pace with rapidly changing technology.
"I don't want to have 200,000 drones somewhere in a stock, and in two months you cannot even use them because they're outdated. So we have to adapt," he said.
Francken also acknowledged Belgium's long-standing underinvestment in defence.
"We were like the worst pupil of the NATO class. We had 1% of GDP in defence spending," he said, adding that spending had since doubled.
"But I cannot do in 18 months what has been neglected for 40 years."
Puzder aims at 'Made in Europe'
European security remains closely tied to the United States, NATO's largest military power.
Relations between Washington and European capitals have faced repeated tensions since Donald Trump returned to the White House and pursued an "America First" agenda.
Matthew Whitaker, the US ambassador to NATO, sought to reassure European allies that Washington remained committed to their security.
"We're not stepping back. We're just asking our allies to step forward and join us," he said. "We have continued to say that we're going to stay engaged in Europe."
Andrew Puzder, the US ambassador to the EU, struck a more confrontational tone, criticising the bloc's push to prioritise "Made in Europe" products in public procurement, including defence.
The policy, which originated in France, has gained support in other EU capitals, although its precise scope remains contested.
"When lives are on the line, capability and availability should determine the solution, not geography," Puzder said.
"One attack by a powerful adversary on a member state, and we'll all be glad that we focused on weapon superiority rather than regional economics."
Puzder instead promoted a "Made in NATO" approach, which would give US defence companies greater access to EU procurement.
"We're stronger when we work together," he said, calling for an alliance that confronts its adversaries with "unity and strength rather than division and self-interest".

articles.title: Bulgarian PM Rumen Radev urges European dialogue with Russia to avert nuclear attack
articles.body:
"We always need to think about the worst-case scenario," Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said at the Euronews' Defence Summit, warning of the risk of a Russian nuclear attack if tensions with Europe escalate.
The European Union should engage diplomatically with Russia to bring the war in Ukraine to an end and avert a devastating nuclear attack, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev told Euronews' Defence and Space Summit.
Russia controls the world's largest nuclear arsenal, with an estimated 4,400 stockpiled warheads, of which 1,796 are strategically deployed.
Radev also criticised Europe's continued deliveries of weapons and ammunition to Ukraine, which he dismissed as a failed "peace by force" strategy.
"There is a limit to just delivering weapons and supporting, because the final peace set-up will be done by diplomacy, not by delivering weapons. So our call is to listen more to each other, to open the lines of communication," Radev said on Wednesday.
"The problem is that no one is raising the question about nuclear risk. Does it exist? Maybe not, I don't know, but this is a risk," he went on.
"We always need to think about the worst-case scenario. Are we prepared for this? Does anybody speak about risk assessment? Does it exist at all? Because we have been trying to achieve a conventional victory over the biggest nuclear power."
Radev referred to the recent statement by Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov, who said a war between Russia and Europe would be "completely different" and "very short", a comment seen as an implicit nuclear threat.
This week, Moscow sent NATO a document threatening to "use the entire arsenal of forces and capabilities at its disposal, including nuclear weapons" to defend its territory from the alliance, according to Reuters.
Radev rejected "this type of speaking" from the Kremlin but urged his fellow European leaders to consider where an escalation might lead.
Tensions have been rising as Moscow ramps up its hybrid attacks against European countries in an attempt to instil societal fear and deter military support for Ukraine.
"There is a nuclear card," the Bulgarian premier said, noting Russia would be prone to play it if weakened or cornered.
"We need to have this into account. We cannot close our eyes (to the fact) that there are nuclear weapons on our continent, there are nuclear weapons in the arsenal of Russia. And this is part of the game calculation."
Since his election earlier this year, Radev has been in the minority that advocates closer diplomatic engagement with Russia to end the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Slovakia, the Czech Republic and Austria have also pushed for dialogue.
Others, however, argue that the Kremlin has little interest in meaningful negotiations and continues to insist on maximalist demands. A short meeting last week between the German foreign minister and Lavrov in New York ended up in bitter recriminations.
The White House's attempts to achieve a temporary ceasefire have all failed. Russia has blocked the Black Sea and launched non-stop airstrikes on Ukrainian cities instead.
Radev seemed undeterred by this track record and insisted Europe should rebalance its "military, economic and diplomatic instruments" in favour of the last strand.
He also pushed back against the label "pro-Russian" that has been attached to his government, which this year vetoed sanctions against Patriarch Kirill.
"The war in Ukraine challenged our critical thinking and realistic approach," he said.
"It challenged our ability to assess the strategic centre of gravity of the opponent. It challenged most of all our ability to design feasible political objectives and to translate them into a sound military strategy and to define a desired end state," he added.
"We have not exhausted the power of diplomacy, and we need to do and to speak more."

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Russia uses drone with warhead designed to cut power pylons for 1st time, Zelensky adviser says
articles.body:
Ukraine war latest: Russia uses drone with warhead designed to cut power pylons for 1st time, Zelensky adviser says
Key developments on Sept. 30:
- Russia uses drone with warhead designed to cut power pylons for first time, Zelensky adviser says
- Drone crashes in Moldova, Romania scrambles fighter jets amid Russian mass attack on Ukraine
- Missile alerts cost Ukraine $45 million for every hour businesses stop, economy minister says
- Zelensky visits Lyman sector, says Operation Vivaldi reclaimed 125 square kilometers
Russia has for the first time used a jet-powered drone equipped with a warhead designed to destroy high-voltage power pylons and steel bridge structures, presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov said on Sept. 30.
The development comes as Moscow renews its large-scale campaign against Ukraine's energy system ahead of winter, launching its heaviest combined attack on energy infrastructure in months overnight on Sept. 30.
"Bad news. Today, the enemy for the first time used a special shaped-charge cutting warhead on a jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)," Beskrestnov, an adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky on defense technologies, wrote on Telegram.
According to Beskrestnov, the warhead was developed specifically to destroy high-voltage pylons and steel bridge structures. It consists of a 40-kilogram main charge and four additional destructive modules.
"I think the enemy plans to attack important high-voltage power transmission lines," he said.
Russia's overnight assault involved nearly 190 attack drones as well as ballistic missiles, Zelensky said. Energy infrastructure in Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast was the primary target, while critical infrastructure was also struck in several other regions.
By the evening, emergency power outages had been introduced in the capital and surrounding region as well as in Chernihiv and Zhytomyr oblasts following repeated Russian attacks on energy infrastructure, according to the Energy Ministry.
The Sept. 30 attack marked a sharp escalation in Russia's renewed campaign against Ukraine's power system.
"Since the summer, there has been practically no day when the enemy has not attacked energy infrastructure. But such a massive and combined attack has occurred for the first time since the end of the last heating season," Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said following the attack.
read also
Drone crashes in Moldova, Romania scrambles fighter jets amid Russian mass attack on Ukraine
A drone flew into Moldovan airspace, crashed outside a village, and exploded in the early hours of Sept. 30 amid a Russian mass attack on Ukraine, Moldova's Defense Ministry said.
The drone entered Moldovan airspace around 5:43 a.m. local time and fell down near the village of Hirbovat in the central Anenii Noi district, where it exploded, according to the ministry.
According to preliminary information, no injuries were reported from the explosion. Moldovan police and army teams were headed to inspect the site.
Romania's Defense Ministry said that its radars detected an aerial target east of Izmail during the night and two F-18 fighter jets of the Spanish air force stationed in the NATO country scrambled as a precaution. No object entered Romanian airspace, the ministry said.
Overnight, Russia attacked across Ukraine with 188 drones, 86 of them jet-powered, as well as with Zircon, Onyx, and Iskander missiles, according to Ukraine's air force. The air force said it shot down or suppressed 5 missiles and 155 drones.
read also
Missile alerts cost Ukraine $45 million for every hour businesses stop, economy minister says
Missile alerts cost Ukraine an estimated $45 million for every hour they force businesses to stop operating, Economy and Environment Minister Oleksandr Kravchenko told the Guardian in an interview published on Sept. 30.
"If people are in a bunker, business stops," Kravchenko told the Guardian.
Kravchenko said prolonged missile alerts can bring large parts of the economy to a standstill as workers move into shelters, with some alerts lasting for hours.
Ukraine introduced a two-tier air raid warning system on Sept. 2 to reduce the economic disruption caused by prolonged alerts. Red alerts are issued when there is a missile threat and require businesses to halt operations and people to seek shelter. Yellow alerts warn primarily of drone threats and allow many businesses to continue operating.
Russia has intensified its aerial campaign against Ukrainian cities and critical infrastructure. Kravchenko said more than half of businesses continue operating during yellow alerts, but those warnings do not mean there is no danger.
On Sept. 28, a Russian jet-powered drone struck the National Academy of Sciences building in central Kyiv during a yellow alert while employees were still inside. The attack killed an aide to former National Security and Defense Council Secretary Volodymyr Horbulin and injured others.
"What we had not fully anticipated was how quickly Russia would develop these jet-powered drones and use them to target everything," Kravchenko said.
Russian attacks have caused an estimated $10 billion in damage to fixed assets in Ukraine this year alone, according to Kravchenko. Steel plants, warehouses, logistics hubs, and data centers have all been hit as Moscow increasingly targets infrastructure supporting the country's economy.
Russia has also stepped up attacks on Ukraine's Black Sea ports and maritime export infrastructure, adding pressure on one of the country's main trade routes.
The government is now discussing ways to allow more private companies to purchase Ukrainian air-defense systems to better protect their facilities, Kravchenko said, while acknowledging that businesses cannot fully shield themselves from Russian missiles and drones.
read also
Zelensky visits Lyman sector, says Operation Vivaldi reclaimed 125 square kilometers
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky visited the command post of the 66th Separate Mechanized Brigade in the Lyman sector running across Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts to award soldiers and meet brigade comannders on Sept. 30.
Zelensky thanked the troops for returning more than 125 square kilometers of territory from Russian occupation to Ukrainian control, in cooperation with other units of the Third Army Corps as part of Operation Vivaldi.
"Thank you for protecting our state, sovereignty, and territorial integrity," he said.
In his talks with the commanders, the President discussed issues of procurement, especially pick-up trucks for brigades, and increasing funding for drones, simplifying procurement, and expanding staffing, Zelensky said. He also highlighted the need for long-range artillery.
Ukrainian forces under the command of the 3rd Army Corps liberated three villages in northern Donetsk Oblast as part of the ongoing Operation Vivaldi, corps commander, Brigadier-General Andrii Biletskyi said on Sept 28.
The villages of Ridkodub, Nove, and Katerynivka were liberated, while full Ukrainian control was restored over Karpivka and Novomykhailivka.
This phase, described as the "third season" of Operation Vivaldi, inflicted over 2,000 Russian losses and saw over 250 Russian soldiers taken prisoner, according to Biletskyi.
The two previous "seasons" of Operation Vivaldi were each announced in similar updates, first on Sept. 15 when the offensive was given its name, and then on Sept. 20, when the liberation of the villages of Shandryholove and Derylove were announced.

articles.title: Explainer-Why Russia's Kaliningrad is a potential flashpoint with NATO
articles.body:
Explainer-Why Russia's Kaliningrad is a potential flashpoint with NATO
Sept 30 - Russia has warned NATO that it would be ready to resort to nuclear weapons if the Western alliance tried to cut off or attack the Russian region of Kaliningrad.
WHERE AND WHAT IS KALININGRAD?
It's a highly militarised exclave - separated from the main mass of Russian territory - that is wedged between NATO members Poland and Lithuania and also borders the Baltic Sea. It has a population of about 1 million and is slightly bigger in area than the US state of Connecticut.
HOW DID IT COME TO BE RUSSIAN?
Kaliningrad, formerly the German city of Königsberg and capital of East Prussia, became part of the Soviet Union after the Red Army captured it in April 1945 and the victorious allies divided East Prussia at the end of World War Two.
WHAT MAKES IT STRATEGICALLY IMPORTANT?
It provides Russia with a platform for air defence, missile and naval forces that can project power deep into northern and central Europe. At the same time, it is a potentially vulnerable pressure point for Moscow because of its boxed-in location between two NATO states and the difficulty of maintaining supply lines or reinforcing it in the event of a war.
WHAT HAS LED TO THE LATEST SPIKE IN TENSIONS?
These have been rising steadily since Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, which led NATO to move decisively to strengthen its eastern flank. The alliance has expanded in the region, with Finland and Sweden joining in 2023 and 2024 respectively.
Russia perceives a growing Western threat to Kaliningrad. In May 2026, it slammed remarks by Lithuania's foreign minister as "verging on insanity" after he said NATO had to show Moscow it was capable of "penetrating the small fortress they've built in Kaliningrad" and razing Russian air defences and missile bases there.
A Western military source told Reuters that dozens of aircraft from NATO members were involved in an unannounced operation in the airspace around Kaliningrad in mid-August, demonstrating the capability to cut off the exclave's radio and radar links as well as its air defences in the event of a conflict with Russia.
In social media posts, Russian embassies in Europe have highlighted what Moscow sees as threatening NATO military movements in the Baltic and hawkish rhetoric on Kaliningrad from policymakers and in the media.
NATO says it has increased its presence in the Baltic Sea partly in response to concerns about threats to critical undersea energy and communications infrastructure. In its response to the Russian warning, it urged Moscow to halt its "increasingly reckless behaviour" and "irresponsible nuclear rhetoric".
WHAT DO EXPERTS FEAR COULD SPARK A CRISIS?
European states have been walking a fine line since 2022 - supporting Ukraine with weapons, intelligence and sanctions against Russia while stopping short of joining the conflict themselves - though Moscow said this week they are already "waging war" against it.
Security analysts say any miscalculation could lead to a direct military confrontation - and Kaliningrad, by virtue of its location, would be a potential flashpoint.
Among the possible triggers could be drone incidents, disruption of critical infrastructure, major new missile deployments or anything perceived by Moscow as amounting to a NATO attempt to impose a blockade on the exclave. REUTERS

articles.title: Russia Sends NATO Formal Nuclear Warning Over Kaliningrad
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Russia Sends NATO Formal Nuclear Warning Over Kaliningrad
Russia privately threatened NATO that it could use nuclear weapons if the alliance attempted to isolate Kaliningrad, Russia’s heavily militarized exclave between Poland and Lithuania, Reuters reported on September 30.
In a diplomatic note sent to NATO and reviewed by Reuters, Moscow accused the alliance of pursuing a “dangerous and reckless course” that carried “high risks of the outbreak of a direct armed conflict.”
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The warning comes amid growing concern over Russian hybrid operations across Europe, including sabotage, arson, cyberattacks, and other hostile activity that governments have linked to Moscow. UNITED24 Media recently detailed how these operations have intensified across the continent.
The document warned that such a confrontation could include “Russian strikes against decision-making centers in the alliance’s member states right from the outset.”
“Russia will be ready to use the entire arsenal of forces and capabilities at its disposal, including nuclear weapons, in order to defend its territory should NATO countries undertake any attempt aimed at isolating the Kaliningrad Region from the rest of the country,” the note stated.
Kaliningrad is a heavily militarized Russian exclave on the Baltic Sea between NATO members Poland and Lithuania. Reuters noted that Moscow has increasingly portrayed allied military activity around the region as a direct threat.
NATO rejected the accusation in a written response also reviewed by Reuters, stating that it is a defensive alliance and that its exercises do not threaten Russian territory.
“None of NATO’s exercises or activities pose a threat to the territory of the Russian Federation,” the alliance stated. “We urge the Russian Federation to refrain from increasingly reckless behaviour towards the Allies and to cease its irresponsible nuclear rhetoric.”
Nikolai Sokov, a Vienna-based nuclear analyst and former Russian diplomat, told Reuters that the warning could reflect growing concern in Moscow over Western arms supplies to Ukraine, sanctions, military exercises, intelligence flights, and possible restrictions on Russian shipping in the Baltic.
“They expect more action, including a blockade of the Baltic Sea — just below the level of war in European calculation, but for them this will be open war,” Sokov stated. “I see a risk of mutual miscalculation.”
Russian embassies in at least three European countries have also issued warnings in recent days accusing NATO of escalating tensions around Kaliningrad, Reuters wrote. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov described the statements as diplomatic reminders to “hotheads in Europe.”
A NATO diplomat characterized the Russian note as another attempt to intimidate European countries and emphasized that the alliance would continue supporting Ukraine. A senior European defense official told Reuters it was the first threat of this kind from Russia since the Cold War and described it as serious.
A day earlier, Russia had already threatened nuclear retaliation if NATO attempted to blockade or attack Kaliningrad, with its embassy in the UK warning that Moscow could respond using “all means available,” including nuclear weapons.
