articles.title: Russian strikes on Ukraine are likely about to get worse, analyst says
articles.body:
Russia is stockpiling weapons to intensify attacks on Ukraine, analysts say
Kyiv — A daytime Russian attack on Ukraine Monday damaged civilian buildings and wounded more than 100 people across the country, according to local authorities.
A drone exploded into the National Academy of Sciences in the heart of Kyiv. Hours later, a second drone damaged a private medical clinic just blocks away. In Dnipro, Ukraine's fourth-largest city, emergency crews rushed to evacuate wounded civilians from a business center also hit in broad daylight.
And yet, the attack could have been much worse.
Ukraine's Air Force said Russia used 124 attack drones from 6:30 a.m. to 6:30 p.m. on Monday — much fewer than in previous barrages this year, which have regularly included more than 500 drones and 50 missiles within the same time frame.
Analysts and Ukrainian officials told CBS News that Russia is stockpiling weapons so that it can launch intensified late-autumn and winter barrages.
During Monday's attack, Russia used primarily "jet-powered drones," a new model of long-range strike drones that fly faster and are harder to intercept. Ukraine's Air Force said that 86 of the 124 drones used in the attack were jet-powered.
Since Russia began deploying the new models in June, Ukraine's interception rate against them is 57% — a sharp drop-off from the military's 90% to 95% success in intercepting older models.
Russia has two models of jet-powered drones, the Geran-4 and Geran-5, and has been stockpiling both. Come Back Alive, a Ukrainian military nonprofit, estimates that Russia will produce 1,200 Geran-4 and 800 Geran-5 in September, and projects those numbers to grow each month.
During his speech at the United Nations General Assembly earlier this month, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia has used just 7,700 jet-powered drones in attacks so far this year.
Viktoriia Chekalina, an analyst at the Come Back Alive Initiatives Center, estimates that Russia has stockpiled 450 to 700 units of the older non-jet-powered drones, the newer jet-powered models and dummy, non-explosive drones known as "Banderols" during each Russian attack this spring and summer.
"Despite the capacity to launch 600-1,000 units in a single massive attack, only about 150-300 drones were actually used," Chekalina told CBS News, explaining that attacks this autumn and winter "could reach around 1,500 units per one raid."
Because Russia has found success striking targets with relatively small barrages of jet-powered drones, it has also managed to save up its cruise and ballistic missiles, which are vastly more expensive and difficult to manufacture.
In the early spring and summer, Russia's attacks on Kyiv included barrages of over 70 cruise and ballistic missiles multiple times per month, according to estimates released by Ukraine's Air Force. In August, Ukraine stopped publicly releasing the numbers of missiles Russia used in each attack, but military analysts told CBS News that there was a drop-off in the number of mass-missile barrages in August and September.
Over this period, Russia has also increased its production of cruise and ballistic missiles. Chekalina said Russia has surpassed its missile production targets by 110% to 120% and estimated that it had stockpiled 130 ballistic missiles by August.
Solutions to countering Russia's ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones remain elusive. Ukraine continues to run dangerously low on American-made PAC-3 ballistic interceptors. And in an address this week, Zelenskyy said that while new defenses against jet-powered drones are being tested, they are not yet ready to be scaled, raising concerns that Ukraine may remain vulnerable heading into winter.
"Russia's goal during winter campaign will be complex: they will focus on attacking electrical and heating infrastructure as they are critical for civilians," Chekalina said. "At the same time, they will use turbojet drones along with missiles on local businesses, warehouses, and other targets."

articles.title: Moscow issues warning to NATO over Russian exclave
articles.body:
Moscow issues warning to NATO over Russian exclave
Increased NATO military exercises near Russia’s Kaliningrad Region and aggressive rhetoric from members of the US-led bloc are raising the risk of a direct armed conflict, Moscow has warned.
Russia has sent NATO a warning stressing its determination to protect the Russian exclave in the Baltic region “with its entire available arsenal,” according to a statement published on Monday by the Russian Embassy in Belgium, which hosts the bloc’s headquarters.
The message alluded to remarks made earlier this month by Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski, who said there are “hardly any troops” in Kaliningrad Region and urged NATO to increase its military posture near Russia’s borders so that Moscow would be “uncertain of what we will do.”
NATO spokesperson Allison Hart confirmed receiving the Russian message and accused Moscow of irresponsible rhetoric.
”We strongly denounce the threat of force, including any irresponsible nuclear rhetoric,” she said.
Western officials have frequently described Russian statements invoking its nuclear deterrent as “blackmail,” while presenting NATO’s own nuclear-sharing arrangements as a pillar of collective defense.
France has offered to discuss the possible deployment of its nuclear weapons in other European NATO countries, arguing that this could reduce the bloc’s dependence on the US. Under NATO’s existing nuclear-sharing arrangements, American nuclear bombs are stored in several European countries, while personnel from non-nuclear member states train for missions involving their potential use.
Russia has repeatedly rejected Western claims that it intends to attack NATO before the end of the decade, describing such warnings as warmongering aimed at persuading voters to support sharply higher military spending.
Moscow, in turn, views NATO’s military preparations as potentially paving the way for an attack on Russia. Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has repeatedly warned that any such conflict would be extremely brief, implying that Moscow could resort to nuclear weapons.
The Russian Embassy in Ireland used more direct language, saying on Tuesday that Moscow is prepared to use nuclear weapons in response to an attempted NATO blockade of Kaliningrad Region and may consider pre-emptive military action in such a crisis.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Wednesday it was “natural for our diplomats to try and remind hotheads in Europe about our doctrinal documents,” in response to the rhetoric coming from Poland and other nations.

articles.title: UAE vice president visits Saudi Arabia in first visit since rift
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
UAE vice president visits Saudi Arabia in first visit since rift
UAE Vice President Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan visited Saudi Arabia on Tuesday and met with the Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and the kingdom's defence minister, the first visit by a senior UAE official to the kingdom since a deep rift emerged between the two Gulf powers last year.
The visit, following an invitation by Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, occurred as Riyadh faces increasing pressure from the Iran-backed Houthis, who have for weeks fired salvos of missiles and drones at the kingdom.
Saudi Arabia has been trying to rally international support to confront the Houthis, but it was not immediately clear if that request extended to the UAE.
The United Arab Emirates was once Saudi Arabia’s main regional partner in the war against the Houthis.
Sheikh Mansour and Prince Khalid discussed topics of mutual interest and ways to enhance cooperation and coordination between the two countries, according to a post by the Saudi defence ministry on X.
Sheikh Mansour, in a separate meeting with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman on Tuesday, reviewed the "fraternal relations" between the two countries and developments in the region, the Saudi state news agency reported.
The UAE and Saudi Arabia's years-long disagreements over everything from geopolitics to oil policy came out into the open in December when an advance by a UAE-backed southern Yemeni separatist group brought it close to Saudi borders.
Saudi Arabia condemned the UAE’s involvement and carried out an airstrike on a UAE-linked weapons shipment at the port of Mukalla in Yemen.
The UAE then announced it had withdrawn all its forces from Yemen but tensions have remained.
Yemen has been caught in a 12-year-long civil war since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa, prompting a Saudi-led military intervention.

articles.title: 'We will defend every inch of NATO territory’: Rutte dismisses Russia’s nuclear threat
articles.body:
Aysu Bicer
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte on Wednesday dismissed Russian nuclear warnings over Kaliningrad, saying Moscow could not win a confrontation with the alliance.
Speaking at the Euronews Defense and Space Summit in Brussels, Rutte said NATO was prepared to defend its territory.
“We will defend every inch of NATO territory. That threat is not there, and if anything happens, we are ready to counter it,” he said.
His comments followed reports that Russia, in a letter, had warned NATO against any attempt to cut off Kaliningrad, its western exclave between Poland and Lithuania, saying it was prepared to use its entire arsenal, including nuclear weapons.
Rutte declined to confirm the contents of the reported letter but rejected the suggestion of an imminent nuclear threat to the Baltic states.
“We are a defensive alliance. Stop the nuclear threat. This is absolutely not called for and not helpful. And particularly stop the war in Ukraine, which is an unprovoked war of aggression against Ukraine,” he said.
Rutte also said Russian President Vladimir Putin could not defeat NATO. “Everybody knows that he can never win against NATO. I don't take this seriously.”
 
Europe’s defense role
Rutte said Russia was suffering heavy losses in Ukraine and claimed 43,000 troops were being killed or seriously wounded each month.
He said Moscow was trying to divide NATO allies and shift attention away from the battlefield.
“If necessary, of course we will defend ourselves. But the most important thing is this is all happening because the war is not going well for him in Ukraine. He wants to divide us. He wants us to lose attention when it comes to Ukraine,” Rutte said.
The NATO secretary general also said Europe must become more capable of handling security threats without relying so heavily on Washington.
“Why are the Americans doing it, taking out the Iranian nuclear capability? Because we can't. But in the future, we have to make sure that as Europeans, we can do this ourselves,” he said.
Rutte said increased European defense spending should eventually allow the continent to assume greater responsibility while keeping the US engaged in NATO.
“Still, the US being involved not only in the nuclear sense but also in the conventional sense, but the Europeans taking much, much more responsibility for the defense of this part of NATO,” he said.

articles.title: Ukraine’s President Zelensky thanks Belgium for the delivery of three F-16 fighter-jets by the end of the year
articles.body:
By the end of the year, Belgium will deliver three F-16 fighter-jets to Ukraine. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky posted plans of the delivery on social media site X. He intends to use an accelerated procedure to make this possible.
Ukraine’s President Zelensky thanks Belgium for delivery of three F-16 fighter-jets by the end of the year
The planned delivery of the three F-16 fighter jets was announced earlier this year by Defence Minister Theo Francken (Flemish nationalist N-VA), both in the Belgian parliament and on the sidelines of President Zelensky’s visit to Brussels.
In total, Belgium is supplying seven F-16 fighter-jets to Ukraine this year: four of them have already been handed over to the Ukrainians but are de facto still at Sabca in Gosselies. At the aerospace company, the aircraft are being used to train Ukrainian technicians to work on them.
These aircraft are too old to fly and can, at best, only be used for spare parts.
The three aircraft that Belgium will deliver by the end of the year can, however, still be used, explains VRT NEWS defence specialist Jens Franssen.
“They have nearly 8,000 flying hours on the clock, which means they are virtually no longer airworthy here.” However, they are still good enough to be used over Ukraine as air defence, to shoot down Russian drones and missiles. “Because that is cheaper than using expensive and scarce Patriot missiles.”

articles.title: Kazakh leader calls Putin ‘outstanding statesman’ in front of Merz (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Kazakh leader calls Putin ‘outstanding statesman’ in front of Merz (VIDEO)
Russian President Vladimir Putin is an “outstanding statesman” suited to leading a great country such as Russia, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said during his visit to Germany on Tuesday.
A former Soviet republic, Kazakhstan is one of Russia’s closest partners in Central Asia.
Tokayev met German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Berlin amid heightened tensions between Germany and Russia over the Ukraine conflict. Germany accused Russia earlier this month of attempting to strike Ukrainian cargo planes with drones at Leipzig/Halle Airport in the German state of Saxony. Moscow rejected the claims as unfounded.
During a joint press conference with Merz, Tokayev said he had “very good relations” with Putin.
“I consider him, one might say, an outstanding statesman. And today I said with a fairly high degree of conviction that President Putin, as a statesman and as a leader, is the most acceptable political figure – strange as that may sound to you – for Central Asia, including Kazakhstan, for Europe, and for the entire world,” Tokayev said in Russian.
“I know him very well. He possesses the qualities that are most essential for the leader of a great country with a complicated history and with its own understanding of the strategic goals it faces,” he added.
💥 Der Präsident Kasachstans, Tokajew, demütigte Merz auf der gemeinsamen Pressekonferenz:
"Wladimir Putin, als Führer der Russischen Föderation, ist die akzeptabelste Figur für Europa und die Welt!" pic.twitter.com/FTFhkZMCtl
Tokayev said that although he favors “freezing” the Ukraine conflict, an immediate end to hostilities is “unrealistic under the current circumstances.”
Kiev has rejected Russia’s ceasefire terms, which include the withdrawal of Ukrainian troops from Russian territory in Donbass and an end to Western military aid to Ukraine. Moscow has argued that Ukraine was not negotiating in good faith and accused Kiev’s European backers of trying to sabotage US-mediated talks.
Speaking at a press conference on Tuesday, Merz reiterated that Germany “will make every effort to continue assisting and supporting Ukraine, not only militarily but also politically, financially and economically.”
Russia has condemned what it described as dangerous rhetoric from the West, with Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov saying last week that the “metastases of an ideology of hatred” were present among EU and NATO members, including Germany.

articles.title: White House Taps Miller to Lead US Space Command
articles.body:
The White House has nominated Lt. Gen. David N. Miller Jr. to lead U.S. Space Command, succeeding Gen. Stephen Whiting, who is expected to retire by January 2027.
A notice of Miller’s nomination for promotion to general appeared in the Congressional Record on Sept. 29, but the notice did not include an assignment. U.S. Space Command and the Space Force both confirmed Sept. 30 that Miller has been tapped for the SPACECOM commander job.
“Congratulations to Lt. Gen. Miller on his nomination to serve as Commander, U.S. Space Command,” Chief of Space Operations Gen. Douglas Schiess said in a statement. “He is an exceptional Guardian who has represented our service with distinction, and we believe he is a strong candidate for this critical joint leadership role.”
Miller, currently the Space Force’s deputy chief of space operations for strategy, plans, programs, and requirements, is a career space operator. He served as commander of Combat Forces Command—then Space Operations Command—from 2024 to 2025, and was director of operations, training, and force development at U.S. Space Command before that. Earlier in his career, he was chief of the Space Control Division within Air Force headquarters, led weapons and tactics development for the 21st Operations Group, and was an intercontinental ballistic missile operator and instructor.
His nomination would make him SPACEOM’s fourth leader since the command was reestablished in 2019, and its third to hail from the Space Force. Charles Galbreath, director of the Mitchell Institute’s Spacepower Advantage Center of Excellence praised Miller as a “straightforward leader” and said he’s glad to see another Guardian in the top SPACECOM job.
“The unique relationship between the space-focused service and combatant command is undeniable,” Galbreath said. “I look forward to seeing that partnership continue to mature under the leadership of Gens. Schiess and Miller.”
If confirmed, Miller would take the reins of the command as the U.S. military’s reliance on space capabilities both in peacetime and in combat takes center stage—and as leaders increasingly emphasize the role of offensive operations in the domain.
Top Pentagon officials have said military space assets and SPACECOM forces played a key role in operations against Iran, providing electronic warfare, navigation, missile warning, and communications capabilities. Speaking at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference on Sept. 14, Air Force Secretary Troy Meink revealed that the Space Force has “space control weapons”—the Defense Department’s most direct acknowledgement to date that the U.S. operates offensive systems in orbit.
Miller will also oversee construction of SPACECOM’s first purpose-built headquarters at Redstone Arsenal in Huntsville, Ala., and the accompanying relocation of personnel and operations from Peterson Space Force Base, Colo. The new facility is in the midst of a phased transition slated to conclude in 2031.
Whiting, the current SPACECOM commander, has been at the helm since January 2024. During his tenure, he has been a vocal proponent of better space domain awareness capabilities, a stronger space “kill chain,” and more dynamic, maneuverable satellites. In a recent speech at the AMOS Conference in Maui, Hawaii, he advocated for improved space-based target tracking and detection capabilities, which he said are foundational to the military’s ability to effectively perform space control operations.
“To be able to negate threats in space, we must be able to find, fix, track, and target those threats,” Whiting said Sept. 16. “Targeting in the space domain is maturing, but it still has a long way to go.”

articles.title: Russian attacks kill at least 6, injure 34 across Ukraine as Kyiv faces another overnight missile, drone attack
articles.body:
Russian attacks kill at least 6, injure 34 across Ukraine as Kyiv faces another overnight missile, drone attack
At least four people were killed and 30 others injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine over the past day, as Russia launched another large-scale missile and drone attack on Kyiv and the surrounding region overnight, local authorities said on Sept. 30.
Russia once again targeted Kyiv overnight, killing at least three people and injuring five others as daily Russian attacks on the capital continued, officials reported.
Just outside the capital in the neighbouring Kyiv Oblast, at least one child was found killed under the rubble of a home in Vyshhorod, Kyiv Oblast Military Administration head Tymur Tkachenko said. A man and a woman also suffered injuries amid the attack.
The Air Force said Russia attacked Ukraine overnight with Zircon and Onyx anti-ship missiles, Iskander-M and S-400 ballistic missiles, and 188 attack drones of various types, including 86 jet-powered drones. Ukrainian air defenses shot down 160 aerial targets, including five missiles and 155 drones, according to the Air Force. Strikes were recorded at 18 locations.
In northern Sumy Oblast, two people were killed and at least 15 others injured in Russian attacks over the past day, local authorities said. A 74-year-old man and a 70-year-old woman were killed after guided aerial bombs struck the Sumy.
In eastern Donetsk Oblast, six people were injured in Russian attacks over the past day, regional Governor Vadym Filashkin said.
In southern Kherson Oblast, five people were injured as Russian forces attacked critical infrastructure and residential areas, regional Governor Oleksandr Prokudin said. Two houses were damaged.
Russian attacks on Dnipropetrovsk Oblast injured a 67-year-old man over the past day, regional authorities said. Russian forces attacked three districts more than 20 times with aerial bombs, drones, and artillery, also causing a fire.

articles.title: Inside the Ukrainian military unit training fighters from China
articles.body:
On the makeshift workbench in the cramped front room of a cottage near the frontlines of the Russia-Ukraine war, there are all the accoutrements of a drone workshop. The walls are lined with pliers and rolls of duct tape; the table is cluttered with screwdrivers and piles of wire. Propped up against the wall are two kamikaze drones. Only one item looks out of place in this Ukrainian village house: a pot of Chinese longjing tea, the leaves wilted from repeated top-ups.
Good tea is one of the many things that Tim misses about his life in China. His parents post monthly supplies to Ukraine. “I think about all of it,” the 44-year-old said, of his home country. “It brings back memories and emotions.”
Tim, who asked to be referred to by his English name, is the lead volunteer in a Ukrainian military unit that this year launched an unusual project: to recruit soldiers from the country seen as Russia’s biggest backer, China.
Many Ukrainian military units have their own brands and public presences as they compete with each other for funding and new recruits. But in this case, the commander of the unit, which focuses on reconnaissance, asked that its identity be withheld because of the sensitivity of the Chinese volunteers project.
“It’s for their sake first and foremost,” said the commander, known by the call sign Muse. “For their own safety and that of their families.”
Muse said five Chinese men who had joined his unit had returned to China after completing their training because of pressure from the Chinese authorities. “We’d put our heart and soul into them,” he lamented. He is fearful that more Chinese soldiers – there are about a dozen so far in the unit – could quit if their identity is revealed. He asked that none of his soldiers’ faces be shown in photographs.
Ukraine’s military is facing an acute manpower shortage. Most of those willing to volunteer to fight have done so, and are fatigued, while some civilian men have gone into hiding to avoid being mobilised. That has turned attention to another pool of potential recruits: foreigners.
There are about 16,000 foreign fighters in Ukraine, making up less than 3% of the armed forces. Before being sacked as defence minister in July, Mykhailo Fedorov passed several reforms designed to make foreign recruitment easier. He predicted that 50% of frontline service members or assault troops could be foreign citizens.
But Chinese volunteers present a unique challenge.
On the one hand, they are uniquely vulnerable to pressure from their own government. The Chinese authorities keep close tabs on their citizens. Chinese law does not specifically forbid citizens from joining foreign armies, but several Chinese volunteers in Ukraine said security services had questioned them or their relatives about their work.
A spokesperson for China’s foreign ministry said it had issued multiple security alerts “to ask Chinese nationals to stay away from areas of armed conflict … and, in particular, avoid participation in any party’s military operations”.
On the other hand, the Chinese soldiers hail from a country that has provided overwhelming support for Russia during the war in Ukraine. Although China claims to be neutral, Beijing has increased trade links with Moscow to record levels since 2022 and provided diplomatic support on numerous occasions. There have also been reports, denied by China, of high-level military cooperation between the two countries.
Some people worry that the Chinese soldiers in Ukraine could provide useful military intelligence to Beijing. An officer from another brigade said he would “think twice” before taking someone from China.
Muse, however, is unbothered. “In this situation, for us commanders, for the Ukrainian people, anyone will do. Because there aren’t enough people,” he said.
Plus, he added, the Chinese work hard. Tim’s main job in the unit is repairing drones. In one week he repaired about 10 Mavics and 15 first-person view (FPV) drones. Impressed, Muse joked that “it is better to have one Chinese person than 10 Ukrainians”.
Chinese volunteers find their way to Muse’s unit through social media and word of mouth. Although there are cursory background checks done by central authorities in Kyiv, Muse entrusts Tim to do the main screening, through a series of interviews.
Tim said the main qualities he looked for were a commitment to Ukraine’s democracy and sovereignty and an ability to communicate well. He added: “I am firmly against accepting someone who is driven simply by hatred for his own country.” He said he had already rejected more than 30 Chinese applicants since joining the unit himself in January, and that he attempted to screen out people with criminal records as well.
But in the murky world of foreign fighters, where people come with stories and claims that are often impossible to verify, dissatisfaction with one’s own country is often a factor.
Vanya, a 36-year-old from central China’s Hubei province, joined the unit over the summer.
Sitting under a trellis of grapevines outside a cottage near the frontlines, stalked by Russian FPV drones, he said life in China had become “suffocating”.
Using a VPN to jump over China’s firewall of internet censorship, he had read about the war in Ukraine, and become familiar with “ideas about democracy and freedom”. That awakening coincided with China’s own economic downturn. His own income, working in home renovations, fell by as much as 50% in some months.
He had long been interested in the military, but was too old to enlist in China. The decision to come to Ukraine “didn’t come out of the blue”, Vanya said. “It was the result of a lot of things building up over time: my weariness of my previous life, my longing for democracy and freedom, as well as my views on Ukraine.”
Other members of the unit claim a more fervent ideology. Nero, a 37-year-old from Fujian province, spent years posting online in support of Ukraine, becoming a well-known influencer. Several of his accounts were deleted; Nero thinks this was in response to his pro-Ukraine views.
He said the blowback he got from suspected Russian spam accounts for his support for Ukraine propelled him towards volunteering.
“I thought: the world shouldn’t be like this. Why should I suffer or go through all this just for speaking the truth?”
His move, which he publicised on social media, led to more harassment. As he arrived in Ukraine, a Russian-language “wanted” poster, which included his real name, date of birth, and picture, appeared online. The poster, which appeared to be faked, accused him of “participating in an armed conflict as a mercenary” and “illegally crossing the state border of the Russian federation”. Nero suspected it was produced by a Chinese propaganda agency working on behalf of Russia, and denied making it himself, saying that revealing his identity endangered him.
Until recently a project manager earning a decent salary in China, Nero is now training to be an FPV drone pilot. “I want people to know that not all Chinese people support Russia’s aggression. Many Chinese people, like me, are kind and want to help Ukraine,” Nero said.
All of the volunteers agreed that scrutiny from the Chinese authorities would make it difficult to return home. “If I go back now, it would be hard to leave again,” said Jinmu, a welder by trade, now working as an electrical engineer, specialising in explosives and batteries.
Whatever contribution they may ultimately make towards peace, or to war, as Chinese nationals their decision is likely to have consequences that last beyond the conflict that they are now a part of. On 23 September, one of their Chinese comrades in the unit was killed in a Russian attack. Upon hearing the news, one volunteer, a doctor, decided to leave. The rest, said Nero, insisted on staying.
Additional research by Illia Dyadik, Yu-chen Li and Artem Mazhulin

articles.title: Russia attacked Kyiv with ballistic missiles: fires broke out, and there were problems with electricity and water supplies
articles.body:
Russia attacked Kyiv with ballistic missiles: fires broke out, and there were problems with electricity and water supplies
Kyiv • UNN
On the night of September 30, ballistic missiles attacked Kyiv. Fires have been reported, along with strikes on energy facilities and disruptions to water and electricity supplies.
The enemy attacked Kyiv with ballistic missiles during the night of Wednesday, September 30. This was reported by UNN.
Details
At 2:47 a.m., the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU Air Force) warned about the movement of ballistic missiles from the Poltava and Chernihiv regions toward the capital.
Kyiv, take shelter immediately. ... All ballistic missiles are heading toward Kyiv
At around 3:00 a.m., the first explosions rang out in the capital. This information was confirmed by Mayor Vitali Klitschko.
There is a fire in the private residential sector of Kyiv's Sviatoshynskyi District. Emergency services are heading to the scene
In turn, the Kyiv City Military Administration reported that a warehouse building was on fire in Kyiv's Holosiivskyi District.
Meanwhile, local social media channels report that four energy infrastructure facilities were attacked in Kyiv and the region tonight; problems with electricity and water supplies are already being observed.
Reminder
The day before, drone debris fell on the Southern Bridge in Kyiv. Local social media channels reported restrictions on road traffic.

articles.title: Trump expected to resume major Iran war after midterms – Axios
articles.body:
Trump expected to resume major Iran war after midterms – Axios
American officials believe US President Donald Trump could order a resumption of major combat operations against Iran after the midterm elections in November, as renewed indirect negotiations produced no results, Axios reported on Tuesday, citing people familiar with the matter.
Qatari mediators, who met separately with US and Iranian negotiators in New York on Monday, are reportedly growing increasingly frustrated that neither side is willing to make concessions.
“It is stuck. The Iranians are asking for things the US can’t accept and the US thinks it is winning so there is no need for compromise,” Axios cited a source as saying.
Trump rejected Iran’s latest proposal last week to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, which handles around a quarter of global seaborne oil and LNG deliveries. He has since denied reports that he was ready to provide sanctions relief and release frozen Iranian assets in exchange for concessions on Iran’s nuclear program. “I offered them NOTHING,” he wrote on Truth Social on Monday.
Democrats are ahead of Republicans by more than ten points nationally in the race for control of the US House of Representatives, according to recent polls by Quinnipiac University and NPR/PBS/Marist.
The war launched by the US and Israel against Iran on February 28 has been unpopular among American voters overall. It sharply divided Trump’s base, with some critics arguing that the president violated his promise of “no new wars” and his stated opposition to “forever wars.”
The relentless bombing campaign failed to subdue Iran and, according to the Pentagon’s inspector general, significantly depleted US ammunition stockpiles. Disruptions to traffic through the Strait of Hormuz continue to drive energy prices, which Trump recently attempted to blame on the Ukraine conflict.
“Donald Trump cannot calm energy markets or conceal the costs of his blockade and hostile policies through show-off and social media posts,” an Iranian security official told RT last week.
According to a recent Fox News poll, 71% of registered voters in the US believed that the Trump administration lacked “a clear strategy for ending the war with Iran,” while 60% said the US had made the wrong decision to launch military action.
The poll also found that 47% of respondents believed military action against Iran would make the US less safe, while 32% said it would make the country safer.

articles.title: Trump’s surrender fantasy: The knot in talks
articles.body:
Trump’s surrender fantasy: The knot in talks
TEHRAN — Iran has received Washington’s response to its latest initiative aimed at ending the seven-month-long conflict that began with unprovoked, joint US-Israeli strikes on February 28, as President Donald Trump remains stubbornly wedded to the delusion that military pressure and economic warfare can force the Islamic Republic into submission.
The US response was submitted to President Masoud Pezeshkian during a Cabinet session on Wednesday by Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, government spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani confirmed.
Addressing the Cabinet, President Pezeshkian reaffirmed Tehran’s principled position on resolving the crisis through diplomacy without compromising fundamental rights.
“We will make every effort to bring the agreement to fruition and will firmly stand up for the rights of the Iranian people,” Pezeshkian said, emphasizing: “The agreement must now be based on a win-win strategy.”
The development follows Araghchi’s return from the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, where Iranian diplomats engaged in indirect exchanges with American representatives while holding intensive consultations on the sidelines with Qatari and Pakistani mediators. Mohajerani noted that Araghchi briefed the Cabinet on these diplomatic engagements, which detailed Iran’s framework for reopening the strategic Strait of Hormuz.
Last week, Araghchi presented a comprehensive seven-point proposal to reopen the waterway within seven days, contingent upon Washington lifting its naval blockade of Iranian ports, unfreezing national assets, and removing illegal sanctions on Iranian oil exports. While Trump hastily dismissed the initiative—claiming Iran was “losing so badly” and that Tehran’s terms “would not be acceptable”—regional mediators have persisted in their efforts to forge a diplomatic resolution based on the reality on the ground.
Paralyzed by strategic deadlock
Tehran views Washington’s mixed signals not as strength, but as profound strategic disorientation. Speaking on Tuesday during a meeting in Tehran with Shahin Mustafayev, Azerbaijan’s Deputy Prime Minister, Major General Mohsen Rezaei, Secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council (SNSC), characterized the US president as trapped in a state of absolute paralysis.
“Trump is caught in a quagmire where he can neither negotiate nor fight,” Rezaei stated. “Iran’s conditions have been conveyed to the United States, but Trump is unable to make a decision, and the United States, out of desperation, has resorted to an air siege in the military war.”
Denouncing the initial February 28 aggression as a blatant violation of international law, Rezaei noted that Iran “powerfully defended itself,” citing the hundreds of precise drone and missile retaliatory strikes conducted by the Iranian Armed Forces against US and Israeli military installations across the region. Tehran has repeatedly cautioned Washington that it will never leave any act of aggression unanswered, demonstrating through seven months of sustained resistance that its deterrence remains fully intact.
This is not the first time Washington has squandered diplomatic off-ramps. Following the collapse of the fragile April 8 ceasefire and the subsequent Islamabad memorandum of understanding (MoU) brokered on June 17, Tehran has demonstrated a readiness to engage in serious diplomacy if national sovereignty is respected. President Pezeshkian reiterated his commitment to seeing the Islamabad MoU come to fruition while safeguarding vital national interests, rejecting US bullying: “We will never bow our head or bend at the knee.”
From military failure to psychological warfare
Having failed to break Iran’s defensive capabilities, the US and Israel have shifted their tactics toward internal disruption. Addressing mayors of major metropolitan centers and provincial capitals on Tuesday, President Pezeshkian pointed out that Washington and Tel Aviv have pivoted toward hybrid subversion after suffering strategic setbacks on the battlefield.
“After failing to force the Iranian people to surrender through military war, enemies have focused their entire plan on creating and intensifying internal divisions,” Pezeshkian cautioned.
Despite this dual track of subversion and rhetoric, the White House continues to escalate coercive measures. On Tuesday, the US Treasury Department unveiled fresh sanctions under its so-called “Operation Economic Outcast,” blacklisting ten individuals and entities across Iran, Hong Kong, and Pakistan over alleged roles in Iran’s defense procurement.
Trump’s search for an off-ramp
However, the coercive campaign has boomeranged disastrously onto the US domestic arena. With US legislative elections just five weeks away, polls indicate that Trump’s war against Iran has been overwhelmingly unpopular from its inception. The disruption of Persian Gulf transit corridors and the subsequent spike in global crude prices have placed immense strain on American households, threatening Republican control of both chambers of Congress.
In a stark illustration of the domestic fallout, California Governor Gavin Newsom suspended the state’s seasonal summer-blend gasoline requirement, directing regulatory bodies to immediately permit the distribution of cheaper winter-blend fuel. In just seven months, Trump’s war has drained over $120 billion in extra fuel expenses from American consumers—imposing an estimated $428 burden on every California household and eroding US economic stability.
With domestic outrage mounting, the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps (IRGC) directly addressed the American public on Tuesday in an unprecedented 26-page open letter, calling on voters to reject the architects of the conflict.
“Remove from power the evil, deceitful, and violent politicians who are responsible for America’s current state,” the IRGC stated, adding: “Make sure your politicians understand that the world has changed.”
While Donald Trump is desperately seeking an off-ramp before voters head to the polls, analysts emphasize that any genuine breakthrough will remain elusive until Washington completely discards the Israeli-instigated illusion that Iran can be coerced into capitulation. Until the White House frees itself from Tel Aviv’s maximalist adventurism and faces strategic realities, its policies will remain locked in the very quagmire of its own making.

articles.title: ‘If people are in a bunker, business stops’: Missile alerts cost Ukraine $45m for every hour they halt businesses
articles.body:
Missile alerts are costing Ukraine an estimated $45m (£34m) for every hour they bring business to a halt, according to the country’s economy minister, as Kyiv searches for ways to keep the economy running under an intensifying Russian bombardment.
Russia has increasingly targeted the infrastructure underpinning Ukraine’s economy, striking industrial sites, warehouses, logistics hubs and datacentres in what Oleksandr Kravchenko, the minister for economy and the environment, described as an effort to “destroy pretty much the entire economy”.
“What we had not fully anticipated was how quickly Russia would develop these jet-powered drones and use them to target everything,” he said, referring to Russia’s use of the new weapons that have pounded Kyiv in recent weeks.
Speaking from the heavily protected government building in Kyiv, Kravchenko, a former McKinsey executive who joined the government in the summer, said the attacks were forcing large parts of the economy into repeated standstills as workers were sent to shelters, with sirens lasting up to 10 hours a day.
“If people are in a bunker, business stops,” he said.
To ease the economic costs, the government recently introduced a new two-tier warning system designed to keep businesses operating during prolonged air raid alerts.
A “red” alert warns of a missile threat and requires people to seek shelter, while a “yellow” warning is used for drone threats, allowing many businesses to remain open.
More than half of businesses were continuing to operate during yellow alerts, Kravchenko said.
But a yellow alert is no guarantee of safety. That danger was made clear on Monday, when a Russian jet-powered drone struck the National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv during a yellow alert, killing two people while staff were still inside working.
It is one of the difficult trade-offs Ukraine faces as it tries to keep normal life moving while protecting people from an escalating campaign of Russian strikes.
Kravchenko said Russian attacks this year alone had caused an estimated $10bn in damage to fixed assets, with steel plants, warehouses, logistics infrastructure and, most recently datacentres, among the targets. Russia has also effectively blockaded Ukraine’s Black Sea ports, which before the blockade carried the bulk of the country’s exports.
The minister believed the government was better prepared this year for what could be the “hardest, the harshest winter” of the war, with further pressure expected on energy supplies, infrastructure and businesses already weakened by months of strikes.
To protect against future strikes, the government is now discussing ways to allow more private companies to purchase Ukraine’s air-defence system, the minister said, although he cautioned that businesses could never fully protect themselves from Russian missiles and drones.
The ongoing damage from strikes has added to an already severe strain on the state’s finances.
The president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has recently put Ukraine’s remaining budget shortfall this year at about $27bn, a figure that has prompted questions among some European governments over how the gap emerged, despite the EU having already agreed a €90bn loan package for Ukraine covering 2026 and 2027.
Kravchenko said the government had since narrowed the shortfall to $20bn through spending cuts and by identifying additional domestic reserves.
Kyiv was now seeking further support from the EU, Japan, Canada and the UK, including potentially bringing forward loans that had been earmarked for next year, Kravchenko said.
“There is very active work with all our international partners to get additional sources of funding,” he said.
Kravchenko dismissed suggestions that the shortfall was the result of mismanagement or corruption. He also said it was not due to excessive spending under former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov, whose drive to overhaul military procurement and rapidly expand Ukraine’s drone programme had made him one of the government’s most prominent reformers before his dismissal in July, a move that triggered street protests.
Instead, he said the gap reflected both weaker-than-expected state revenues and the rising cost of waging the war.
“The cost of war is simply increasing,” he said, pointing to the need for more air-defence systems and for Ukraine to accelerate development of drones capable of intercepting Russia’s new jet-powered weapons.
But high-profile corruption scandals have also reached Zelenskyy’s inner circle, straining trust in the government both at home and among western donors.
A recent poll by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology found that corruption in government was the most cited concern among Ukrainians, named by 50% of respondents, ahead of mass missile and drone strikes at 40%. The same survey found that 72% believed Zelenskyy bore personal responsibility for corrupt actions by people around him.
Kravchenko said progress had been made to tackle the issue but admitted that Ukraine faced both corruption itself and a persistent perception problem both inside Ukraine and abroad.
“I very much appreciate the pressure of European partners on reforms,” he said, adding that Ukraine also needed to tackle perceptions of corruption at home and abroad.
Ukraine’s external financing needs for 2027 are estimated at $52.6bn, but only about $20bn has so far been secured, according to the minister, with further tax rises and spending cuts under discussion.
Asked whether the rise of parties sceptical of support for Ukraine in France and Germany could weaken western commitment to Kyiv, he said: “Am I worried? I think I should be, probably.”
“The overall fatigue is increasing in Europe,” he added.

articles.title: “We cannot rule out civilian casualties” – SAB director warns of Russia’s next move
articles.body:
Russia, unable to defeat Ukraine, is raising the stakes in Europe, and civilian casualties cannot be ruled out, Director of Latvia’s Constitution Protection Bureau (SAB) Egils Zviedris said in an interview with LETA.
SAB has been warning about the escalation of Russia’s unconventional warfare since early spring. According to Zviedris, Russia has been unable to achieve its stated objective of victory in the war against Ukraine and is therefore escalating the situation in Europe in response to Western support for Ukraine.
This escalation includes hybrid threats such as cyberattacks, physical acts of sabotage and information warfare. Russia is escalating the situation because it has failed to weaken Western support for Ukraine or secure an easing of sanctions, Zviedris explained.
This has resulted in incidents such as drones carrying explosives at Leipzig Airport and acts of sabotage targeting railway lines in European countries.
“Russia is raising the stakes, and unfortunately, we cannot rule out civilian casualties,”
the head of Latvia’s intelligence service stressed.
Zviedris pointed out that, so far, false-flag operations are essentially the only type of operation Russia has not carried out in Europe, as other forms of hostile activity have already occurred.
He recalled that Latvia has experienced the desecration of monuments and an arson attack on the Museum of the Occupation of Latvia, while Russian opposition figures living in Lithuania have been attacked. Recent warnings by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk about threats from Russia were specifically related to the risk of false-flag operations, Zviedris said.
He also pointed to a recent Russian attack on a Ukrainian passenger train just two kilometres from the Polish border.
“Tusk was therefore warning about Russian attacks near the borders of NATO countries.
Such statements are a warning to Russia that we see what it is doing near the borders of our countries and that we will not tolerate it,” the SAB director added.
Zviedris also recalled that Latvia has requested the deployment of four NATO fighter jets to the country for the duration of the Saeima election, a request to which Germany has responded.
The move is intended to prevent possible provocations, such as unidentified flying objects entering Latvian airspace, which could subsequently fuel speculation about the legitimacy of the election process.
“So the threat from Russia is real, and as the aggressor is unable to achieve its objectives in Ukraine, the stakes are being raised,” Zviedris added.

articles.title: Ukraine names 23 Russian companies manufacturing missiles for Pantsir air defence system
articles.body:
Ukraine names 23 Russian companies manufacturing missiles for Pantsir air defence system
Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) has released information on 23 Russian companies involved in a manufacturing partnership to produce 95Ya6 surface-to-air guided missiles used in Russian Pantsir surface-to-air missile and anti-aircraft artillery systems.
Source: Defence Intelligence of Ukraine on Telegram; War&Sanctions portal
Details: DIU said 95Ya6 missiles serve as the primary medium-range ammunition for various Pantsir modifications.
Quote from DIU: "A key role in the creation of these missiles is played by the Design Bureau of Instrument Making named after Academician A. G. Shipunov JSC – the main developer and manufacturer of 95Ya6 missiles. The company is known for its involvement in producing armaments for Orion unmanned systems, Krasnopol guided artillery shells and cannons for Sukhoi fighters."
Details: Crucially, about one-third of the companies disclosed by DIU are not currently subject to sanctions by any member of the sanctions coalition. These include:
- Komponent Plant JSC – manufacturer of non-contact target sensors for 95Ya6 missiles
- Saratov Electrical Instrument Manufacturing Plant named after Sergo Ordzhonikidze PJSC – producer and supplier of emitter and power supply units for these missiles
- Tambov Plant Elektropribor PJSC – manufacturer of flight-control actuators for the 95Ya6.
Quote: "DIU emphasises that to effectively weaken the aggressor's military potential, it is vital to impose coordinated restrictions on businesses that produce the full range of Russian weapons, rather than focusing solely on offensive systems."
For reference: Pantsir is a family of Russian self-propelled short-range surface-to-air missile and anti-aircraft artillery systems designed to protect key military and industrial facilities from aerial threats. Russia also uses these systems to reinforce air defence at low and ultra-low altitudes and to counter massed aerial attacks.
Details: DIU noted that Russian forces have been deploying Pantsir systems on rooftops in Moscow since 2023. This year, they were also spotted deploying another variant, the Pantsir-SMD-E. According to DIU, unlike earlier variants, this model is equipped with small TKB-1055 Gvozd anti-drone missiles instead of autocannons.
Background: DIU released an interactive 3D model and information on over 50 companies involved in the production of the Russian Pantsir-S1 air defence gun and missile system.

articles.title: Latvia could host nuclear weapons if NATO chooses to deploy them, president says
articles.body:
Nuclear weapons could be stationed in Latvia if NATO decides to do so and the need arises, Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs said.
“Our laws pose no legal obstacles to stationing nuclear weapons in Latvia,” he said.
No specific talks on stationing nuclear weapons in Latvia are currently underway, however, Rinkēvičs said.
On September 29, Britain proposed extending its nuclear umbrella to the Baltic and Nordic countries. The proposal calls for an additional deterrent that would operate independently of NATO. British nuclear submarines would play a key role in providing that deterrent.
In mid-September, Lithuania’s parliament backed a bill to lift the constitutional ban on stationing nuclear weapons in the country. Amid debate over the bill, the Kremlin said Lithuania would be “in the crosshairs” of Russian nuclear weapons if it hosted a nuclear arsenal.
It emerged on September 30 that Russia had sent NATO a document warning that it could use nuclear weapons if there were an attempt to “isolate the Kaliningrad region from the rest of the country.”

articles.title: ADF neutralizes five ballistic missiles, 155 Russian drones used to attack Ukraine overnight
articles.body:
ADF neutralizes five ballistic missiles, 155 Russian drones used to attack Ukraine overnight
According to Ukrinform, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine said this on Telegram.
Starting at 18:00 on Tuesday, September 29, Russian forces attacked with Zircon/Oniks anti-ship missiles launched from Kursk region, Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles launched from Voronezh and Bryansk regions, and 188 attack UAVs, including 86 jet-powered drones, of the Shahed type, as well as Gerbera and Parody decoy drones. The drones were launched from the areas of Orel, Millerovo, Kursk, Primorsko-Akhtarsk in Russia, temporarily occupied Donetsk, as well as Hvardiiske and Chauda in temporarily occupied Crimea.
The main direction of the attack was the Kyiv region.
The air assault was repelled by aircraft, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare units, unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine's Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 08:00 on Wednesday, September 30, Ukrainian air defense had shot down or suppressed 160 targets: five Iskander-M/S-400/Zircon/Oniks ballistic missiles and 155 drones.
Hits were recorded at 18 locations.
The attack was ongoing, with several enemy drones still in Ukrainian airspace.
As Ukrinform reported, two people were killed and four injured in Kyiv as a result of the Russian missile and drone attack on September 30.
A child was killed in Vyshhorod, Kyiv region, as a result of the Russian combined attack, and there were also casualties.

articles.title: Russian attack kills two, wounds four in Kiev
articles.body:
Ukraine's air defences are seen in action during a missile and drone strike on Kyiv amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine early on September 30, 2026. (AFP Photo)
Russian strikes killed four in and around Ukraine’s capital on Sept. 30, the authorities said, in a barrage of attacks which hit the city’s energy infrastructure and cut power.
Heavy explosions rang out across Kiev throughout a night of almost continuous air alerts warning people to take cover in bomb shelters from ballistic and cruise missiles backed up by drones.
Kiev, home to some 3 million people, has faced several nights of sustained aerial barrages, as well as increasing daytime strikes in an escalation of the more than four-and-a-half-year-long war.
In Moscow, Russia’s Defense Ministry said it had conducted “a massive missile and drone strike” on Kiev and the surrounding region that targeted the power infrastructure.
Ukraine’s main energy provider DTEK confirmed that the grid was damaged and supplies were affected.
“DTEK’s power engineers managed to quickly restore electricity to 8,000 households,” the company said in a statement, calling it “another difficult night for the capital.”
Strikes on Sept. 30 hit residential buildings and businesses, sparking fires and widespread damage to property and cars, the authorities said.
City mayor Vitali Klitschko said a driver at local utility firm KievTeploEnergo was killed when a warehouse was hit, while two others were killed elsewhere.
The emergency services said a child was found dead under the rubble of a residential building that was destroyed in the wider Kiev region.
Russia has been deploying newer jet-powered drones that move faster and are harder to intercept than the traditional models, which are based on Iranian Shaheds.
U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Sept. 29 said he was “alarmed” by the scale of the escalating daily attacks in Ukraine and civilian casualties on both sides.
